method: Lectio Edition (SDIT): a faithful modern-English rendering of Shakespeare's Early Modern English — verse lines kept, imagery and wordplay kept, only genuine language-friction removed (archaic grammar, dead idiom, lost allusion). Not a paraphrase; the original is the default edition and always one tap away. In progress, act by act.
sourcesCited: Shakespeare's text (the conflated Second Quarto / First Folio Hamlet, public domain)
the OED and a standard glossarial edition (Arden, consulted, not quoted) for archaic senses
overview: The Lectio Edition opens Hamlet to readers who bounce off the Early Modern English — keeping the verse, the metaphors, and the famous lines, but clearing away the archaic grammar and dead idiom that block the meaning. A companion to Shakespeare's own words, not a replacement.
introduction: With Shakespeare, unlike Homer or Dante, the English is the art — so this edition is the lightest of touches. It keeps the verse lines and nearly all of Shakespeare's words; it only steps in where the language itself blocks a modern reader: an archaic construction untangled, a dead word glossed in place, an inverted clause set right. The original is the default reading here; this is the on-ramp, always a tap away.

divergences.note: Hamlet's dismissive interjection when Polonius announces stale news. "Buzz" was an Elizabethan noise of contempt — "old news, I've heard it" — but to a modern ear "buzz, buzz" reads as a sound effect, not a put-down. Rendered as a scoffing "Bah, bah" to preserve the dismissal; the original is one tap away for those who want the period flavor.

divergences.phrase: an aerie of children, little eyases
divergences.older: an aerie of children, little eyases, that cry out on the top of question
divergences.lectio: a whole nestful of children, little fledgling hawks, who shriek out their lines at the top of their range
divergences.note: A topical jab at the boys' acting companies (the "War of the Theatres", c. 1600) whose popularity was siphoning audiences from the adult players. "Eyas" is a nestling hawk taken to be trained; the dead falconry term is glossed in place as "fledgling hawks" so the bird-of-prey image (and the hawk/handsaw motif a few lines later) survives, rather than being flattened to "child actors."

"Mobled" — muffled, with the head wrapped — is a rare word, and the scene makes a point of it: Hamlet stops on it ("'The mobled queen'?") and Polonius approves ("'Mobled queen' is good"). Replacing it with the ordinary "muffled" would leave their exchange about nothing, so Shakespeare's word is kept and its sense glossed in the margin.

divergences.phrase: To be, or not to be, that is the question
divergences.older: To be, or not to be, that is the question: ... his quietus make / With a bare bodkin? Who would these fardels bear ... from whose bourn / No traveller returns
divergences.lectio: To be, or not to be, that is the question: ... settle his account / with a bare dagger? Who would carry these burdens ... from whose border / no traveller returns
divergences.note: The most famous speech in English is kept essentially verbatim. The opening line, 'slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,' 'a sea of troubles,' 'this mortal coil,' 'the undiscovered country,' and 'conscience does make cowards of us all' are untouched. Only four pure-vocabulary blanks a modern reader stalls on were cleared, each preserving the meter: 'quietus make / With a bare bodkin' became 'settle his account / with a bare dagger' (bodkin = a short dagger; quietus = the settling of a debt); 'fardels' became 'burdens'; 'bourn' became 'border'; and 'contumely' became 'contempt.' Nothing was added, cut, or reordered.

divergences.phrase: The lady protests too much, methinks
divergences.older: The lady protests too much, methinks.
divergences.lectio: The lady protests too much, methinks.
divergences.note: Kept word for word. The line is known with "methinks," and the word is still understood by every reader, so there is no friction to clear. The proverbial form ('doth protest too much') comes from later quotation; the bundled Folio text reads 'protests,' which is preserved.

divergences.phrase: I must be cruel, only to be kind
divergences.older: I must be cruel, only to be kind: / Thus bad begins, and worse remains behind.
divergences.lectio: I must be cruel, only to be kind. / Thus bad begins, and worse remains behind.
divergences.note: Kept verbatim — the line carries no archaic friction and is among the act's signature phrases, so it is left exactly as written, including the rhymed couplet that closes the thought.

divergences.phrase: owl was a baker's daughter / know not what we may be
divergences.older: They say the owl was a baker's daughter. Lord, we know what we are, but know not what we may be.
divergences.lectio: They say the owl was a baker's daughter. Lord, we know what we are, but know not what we may be.
divergences.note: Kept verbatim. The owl alludes to a folk tale in which Christ, refused bread, turns a baker's daughter into an owl — a fable of sudden, undeserved transformation. Ophelia, broken, applies it to herself: we know our present selves but not what we may become. Too famous, and too exact, to touch.

divergences.older: Of nothing. Bring me to him. Hide fox, and all after.
divergences.lectio: Of nothing. Bring me to him. Hide fox, and all after.
divergences.note: Left intact. It is the call of a children's hunting game — our hide-and-seek, the hider being the 'fox' and the rest the hounds in pursuit. Hamlet, mad in act and dead-serious underneath, runs out as if starting the chase; modernizing the tag would flatten both the play-cry and the threat.

divergences.phrase: When these are gone, / The woman will be out
divergences.older: When these are gone, / The woman will be out.
divergences.lectio: When these are gone, / the woman in me will be done.
divergences.note: Laertes calls weeping the 'woman' in him; once his tears are spent, that softness leaves and the man returns. 'The woman will be out' reads today as 'will emerge,' the reverse of his meaning, so the Vernacular makes the sense explicit — the womanish grief is what ends — while keeping his clipped, embarrassed tone.

divergences.older: It must be _se offendendo_, it cannot be else. ... argal, she drowned herself wittingly.
divergences.lectio: It must be _se offendendo_, it can't be otherwise. ... argal, she drowned herself on purpose.
divergences.note: The gravedigger's law-Latin is mangled on purpose, and the mangling is the joke. "Se offendendo" is his blunder for the legal "se defendendo" (in self-defense) — he says, in effect, "self-offense" — and "argal" is his garbling of the logician's "ergo" (therefore). Both are kept verbatim, because correcting them would erase the comedy of a clown aping the courtroom; only the surrounding prose is eased. His prose stays prose throughout the scene.

divergences.phrase: Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio
divergences.older: Alas, poor Yorick. I knew him, Horatio, a fellow of infinite jest, of most excellent fancy.
divergences.lectio: Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio — a fellow of infinite jest, of most excellent imagination.
divergences.note: The most quoted line in the scene is kept verbatim, including the popular exclamation point. Only one pure-vocabulary word is glossed in place: "fancy" in its Elizabethan sense is the faculty of imagination (not a modern whim), so it is rendered "imagination" to keep Hamlet's praise of Yorick's wit landing as praise. "Infinite jest" is untouched.

divergences.phrase: there's a divinity that shapes our ends / the readiness is all / The rest is silence
divergences.older: There's a divinity that shapes our ends, / Rough-hew them how we will. ... The readiness is all. ... The rest is silence.
divergences.lectio: there's a divinity that shapes our ends, / rough-hew them how we will. ... The readiness is all. ... The rest is silence.
divergences.note: The act's three signature lines are kept word for word, and so is "rough-hew them how we will," which carries no archaic friction. Around them only friction was cleared: in the sparrow speech "we defy augury" became "we defy omens" and "to leave betimes" became "to leave early," while "The readiness is all" and "a special providence in the fall of a sparrow" stand untouched. Hamlet's last words, "The rest is silence," are left exactly as written, with the broken "which have solicited—" before it kept as a true unfinished thought, dashed off as he dies.

books.label: Act I
paragraphs: SCENE I. Elsinore. A platform before the Castle.
Enter Francisco and Barnardo, two sentinels.

BARNARDO
Who's there?

FRANCISCO
No—you answer me. Stand, and reveal yourself.

BARNARDO
Long live the King!

FRANCISCO
Barnardo?

BARNARDO
The same.

FRANCISCO
You come right on the stroke of your hour.

BARNARDO
It's just struck twelve. Get to bed, Francisco.

FRANCISCO
For this relief, many thanks. It's bitter cold,
and I am sick at heart.

BARNARDO
Have you had a quiet watch?

FRANCISCO
Not a mouse stirring.

BARNARDO
Well, good night.
If you do meet Horatio and Marcellus,
the partners of my watch, bid them make haste.
Enter Horatio and Marcellus.

FRANCISCO
I think I hear them. Stand, there! Who's that?

HORATIO
Friends to this country.

MARCELLUS
And loyal men to the Dane.

FRANCISCO
Good night to you.

MARCELLUS
Oh, farewell, honest soldier. Who has relieved you?

FRANCISCO
Barnardo has my place. Good night to you.
[_Exit._]

MARCELLUS
Hey there, Barnardo!

BARNARDO
What—is Horatio there?

HORATIO
A piece of him.

BARNARDO
Welcome, Horatio. Welcome, good Marcellus.

MARCELLUS
So, has this thing appeared again tonight?

BARNARDO
I have seen nothing.

MARCELLUS
Horatio says it's only our imagination,
and won't let belief take hold of him
about this dreaded sight we've seen twice.
So I've begged him to come along
and keep watch with us through the minutes of this night,
so that if this apparition comes again
he can confirm our eyes, and speak to it.

HORATIO
Tut, tut, it won't appear.

BARNARDO
Sit down awhile,
and let us once again assail your ears,
so fortified against our story,
with what we two nights have seen.

HORATIO
Well, let's sit down,
and let us hear Barnardo speak of this.

BARNARDO
Just last night,
when that same star, westward from the pole,
had traveled its course to light that part of heaven
where now it burns—Marcellus and myself,
the bell just then striking one—

MARCELLUS
Hush, stop—look where it comes again.
Enter Ghost.

BARNARDO
In the same shape, like the King who's dead.

MARCELLUS
You're a scholar—speak to it, Horatio.

BARNARDO
Doesn't it look like the King? Look at it, Horatio.

HORATIO
Most like. It harrows me with fear and wonder.

BARNARDO
It wants to be spoken to.

MARCELLUS
Question it, Horatio.

HORATIO
What are you, that lay claim to this hour of night,
together with that fair and warlike form
in which the majesty of buried Denmark
once marched? By heaven, I command you, speak.

MARCELLUS
It is offended.

BARNARDO
See, it stalks away.

HORATIO
Stay! Speak, speak! I command you, speak!
[_Exit Ghost._]

MARCELLUS
It's gone, and will not answer.

BARNARDO
How now, Horatio! You tremble and look pale.
Is this not something more than imagination?
What do you make of it?

HORATIO
Before my God, I could not have believed this
without the solid, true witness
of my own eyes.

MARCELLUS
Is it not like the King?

HORATIO
As you are like yourself.
That was the very armor he had on
when he fought the ambitious King of Norway;
so he frowned once, when in an angry parley
he struck the sledded Poles down on the ice.
It's strange.

MARCELLUS
Twice before, and exactly at this dead hour,
with soldier's stride he has passed by our watch.

HORATIO
What to make of it exactly, I don't know;
but in the broad sweep of my opinion,
this forebodes some strange upheaval in our state.

MARCELLUS
All right, sit down, and tell me—whoever knows—
why this strict and watchful guard
works the people of this land so hard each night;
and why this daily casting of bronze cannon,
and foreign trade for tools of war;
why this conscription of shipwrights, whose harsh labor
doesn't even spare the Sunday from the week.
What could be coming, that this sweating haste
makes night a fellow-laborer with the day?
Who can inform me?

HORATIO
That I can do—
at least, the rumor goes like this. Our late King,
whose image just now appeared to us,
was, as you know, by Fortinbras of Norway—
spurred on by a most jealous pride—
dared to single combat; and our valiant Hamlet
(for so this side of the known world esteemed him)
slew this Fortinbras; who by a sealed agreement,
well ratified by law and heraldry,
forfeited, with his life, all those his lands
that he possessed, to the conqueror.
Against this, an equal portion
was staked by our King; which would have passed
to the inheritance of Fortinbras
had he been the victor—just as by that same compact,
and the terms of the article drawn up,
his lands fell to Hamlet. Now, sir, young Fortinbras,
of untested mettle, hot and full,
has, in the outskirts of Norway, here and there,
scraped up a band of lawless desperadoes,
paid in food and rations, for some venture
that takes some nerve; which is no other,
as it appears clearly to our state,
than to recover from us, by strong hand
and forced terms, those same lands
so lost by his father. And this, I take it,
is the main reason for our preparations,
the source of this our watch, and the chief cause
of this headlong haste and bustle in the land.

BARNARDO
I think it's nothing other than just that.
It may well fit, that this ominous figure
comes armed through our watch so like the King
who was, and is, the very point of these wars.

HORATIO
It's a speck to trouble the mind's eye.
In the highest and most flourishing days of Rome,
a little before the mightiest Julius fell,
the graves stood empty, and the shrouded dead
did squeak and gibber in the Roman streets;
stars trailing fire, and dews of blood,
blights upon the sun; and the moist star,
upon whose influence Neptune's empire stands,
was sick almost to doomsday with eclipse.
And the very same omens of fierce events—
as heralds always coming before the fates,
and prologue to the doom on its way—
heaven and earth together have shown
to our own region and countrymen.
Re-enter Ghost.

HORATIO
But wait, look! See, where it comes again!
I'll cross its path, though it strike me dead. Stay, illusion!
If you have any sound, or use of voice,
speak to me.
If there is any good thing to be done
that may bring you ease, and grace to me,
speak to me.
If you are privy to your country's fate,
which, perhaps, foreknowing might avoid—
oh, speak!
Or if you have hoarded up, in your life,
plundered treasure in the womb of earth
(for which, they say, you spirits often walk in death),
speak of it. Stay, and speak!
[_The cock crows._]

HORATIO
Stop it, Marcellus!

MARCELLUS
Shall I strike at it with my spear?

HORATIO
Do, if it won't stand still.

BARNARDO
It's here!

HORATIO
It's here!
[_Exit Ghost._]

MARCELLUS
It's gone!
We do it wrong, it being so majestic,
to offer it this show of violence,
for it is like the air, beyond all wounding,
and our useless blows are spiteful mockery.

BARNARDO
It was about to speak, when the cock crowed.

HORATIO
And then it flinched, like a guilty thing
at a dreaded summons. I have heard
that the cock, the trumpet of the morning,
with his high and shrill-sounding throat
wakes the god of day; and at his warning,
whether in sea or fire, in earth or air,
the wandering and straying spirit hurries
back to its confine. And of the truth of this,
this very thing just gave the proof.

MARCELLUS
It faded at the crowing of the cock.
Some say that always, just before the season comes
in which our Savior's birth is celebrated,
the bird of dawn sings all night long;
and then, they say, no spirit dares stir abroad,
the nights are wholesome, then no planets blast,
no fairy steals, no witch has power to charm—
so holy and so gracious is the time.

HORATIO
So I have heard, and partly believe it.
But look, the morning, robed in russet mantle,
walks over the dew of that high eastern hill.
Let's break off our watch; and, by my advice,
let us tell what we have seen tonight
to young Hamlet—for, upon my life,
this spirit, silent to us, will speak to him.
Do you agree we should inform him of it,
as our love requires, and our duty fits?

MARCELLUS
Let's do it, I beg you; and I know this morning
where we shall find him most conveniently.
[_Exeunt._]
SCENE II. Elsinore. A room of state in the Castle.
Enter Claudius King of Denmark, Gertrude the Queen, Hamlet, Polonius, Laertes, Voltemand, Cornelius, Lords and Attendant.

KING
Though the memory of our dear brother Hamlet's
death is still fresh, and though it suited us
to hold our hearts in grief, and our whole kingdom
to be drawn together in one brow of woe;
yet good sense has so far wrestled with nature
that we now think of him with wisest sorrow,
while remembering ourselves as well.
Therefore our former sister, now our queen,
the imperial partner in this warlike state,
we have—as if with a defeated joy,
with one eye smiling and one eye dropping tears,
with mirth at the funeral and a dirge at the wedding,
weighing delight and grief in equal scale—
taken to wife; nor in this have we ignored
your better wisdoms, which have freely gone
along with this affair. For all, our thanks.
Now, you should know that young Fortinbras,
holding a low opinion of our worth,
or thinking that, by our late dear brother's death,
our state is disjointed and out of frame,
allied with this dream of his advantage,
has not failed to pester us with messages
demanding the surrender of those lands
lost by his father, with all bonds of law,
to our most valiant brother. So much for him.
Now for ourself, and for this present meeting:
here is the business. We have written
to Norway, uncle of young Fortinbras—
who, sick and bedridden, scarcely hears
of this his nephew's plans—to put a stop
to his advance; since the levies,
the musters, and the full forces are all drawn
from Norway's subjects. And we now dispatch
you, good Cornelius, and you, Voltemand,
to carry this greeting to old Norway,
giving you no further personal power
to deal with the King than the scope
of these detailed articles allows.
Farewell; and let your haste reflect your duty.

CORNELIUS and VOLTEMAND
In this, and all things, we will show our duty.

KING
We doubt it not. Heartily, farewell.
[_Exeunt Voltemand and Cornelius._]

KING
And now, Laertes, what's the news with you?
You told us of some request. What is it, Laertes?
You cannot speak of anything reasonable to the Dane
and waste your breath. What could you ask, Laertes,
that would not be my offer before your asking?
The head is no more natural to the heart,
the hand no more useful to the mouth,
than the throne of Denmark is to your father.
What would you have, Laertes?

LAERTES
My dread lord,
your leave and favor to return to France—
from which, though I came willingly to Denmark
to do my duty at your coronation;
yet now, that duty done, I must confess
my thoughts and wishes bend again toward France,
and bow before your gracious leave and pardon.

KING
Have you your father's leave? What says Polonius?

POLONIUS
He has, my lord, wrung from me my reluctant leave
by tireless petition; and at last
I sealed my hard consent upon his will.
I beg you, give him leave to go.

KING
Take your good hour, Laertes; the time is yours,
and spend it as your best graces will!
But now, my nephew Hamlet, and my son—

HAMLET
[_Aside._] A little more than kin, and less than kind.

KING
How is it that the clouds still hang on you?

HAMLET
Not so, my lord. I am too much in the sun.

QUEEN
Good Hamlet, cast off that nighttime color,
and let your eye look on Denmark like a friend.
Don't forever, with your lowered lids,
search for your noble father in the dust.
You know it's common—all that lives must die,
passing through nature on to eternity.

HAMLET
Ay, madam, it is common.

QUEEN
If it is,
why does it seem so particular with you?

HAMLET
Seems, madam? No, it is. I know not "seems."
It's not just my black cloak, good mother,
nor the customary suits of solemn black,
nor gusty sighing of forced breath,
no, nor the flowing river in the eye,
nor the downcast look upon the face,
together with all forms, moods, shows of grief,
that can express me truly. These indeed seem,
for they are actions that a man might play;
but I have that within which passes show;
these are merely the trappings and the suits of woe.

KING
It's sweet and admirable in your nature, Hamlet,
to pay these mourning duties to your father;
but you must know, your father lost a father;
that father lost, lost his; and the survivor, bound
in a son's obligation, for some time
to observe a dutiful grief. But to persist
in stubborn mourning is a course
of ungodly obstinacy. It's unmanly grief.
It shows a will most disobedient to heaven,
a heart unfortified, a restless mind,
an understanding simple and untaught.
For what we know must happen, and is as common
as the most ordinary thing to the senses—
why should we, in our peevish resistance,
take it to heart? Shame—it's a fault to heaven,
a fault against the dead, a fault to nature,
most absurd to reason, whose constant theme
is the death of fathers, and which has always cried,
from the first corpse to the man who died today,
"This must be so." We beg you, throw to earth
this useless grief, and think of us
as of a father; for let the world take note,
you are the closest in line to our throne,
and with no less nobility of love
than that which the dearest father bears his son
I hold toward you. As for your intention
to go back to school in Wittenberg,
it runs entirely against our wish;
and we beg you, bring yourself to stay
here in the cheer and comfort of our eye,
our foremost courtier, nephew, and our son.

QUEEN
Let not your mother lose her prayers, Hamlet.
I beg you, stay with us; do not go to Wittenberg.

HAMLET
I shall, as best I can, obey you, madam.

KING
Why, that's a loving and a fair reply.
Be like ourself in Denmark. Madam, come;
this gentle, unforced agreement of Hamlet's
sits smiling at my heart; and in its honor,
no merry toast that Denmark drinks today
but the great cannon shall announce it to the clouds,
and the King's carousing the heavens shall echo back,
resounding earthly thunder. Come away.
[_Exeunt all but Hamlet._]

HAMLET
Oh, that this too, too solid flesh would melt,
thaw, and resolve itself into a dew!
Or that the Everlasting had not fixed
his law against self-slaughter. O God! O God!
How weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable
seem to me all the uses of this world!
Shame on it! Oh, shame! It's an unweeded garden
gone to seed; things rank and gross in nature
possess it utterly. That it should come to this!
But two months dead—no, not so much, not two:
so excellent a king, who was to this one
Hyperion to a satyr; so loving to my mother
that he would not let the winds of heaven
touch her face too roughly. Heaven and earth!
Must I remember? Why, she would cling to him
as if her appetite had only grown
by what it fed on; and yet, within a month—
let me not think on it—Frailty, thy name is woman!—
a little month, before the very shoes were old
in which she followed my poor father's body,
like Niobe, all tears—why she, even she—
O God! A beast that has no power of reason
would have mourned longer—married my uncle,
my father's brother; but no more like my father
than I am like Hercules. Within a month,
before the salt of her most unrighteous tears
had left the redness in her chafed eyes,
she married. Oh, most wicked speed, to rush
with such dexterity to incestuous sheets!
It is not, nor can it ever come to good.
But break, my heart, for I must hold my tongue.
Enter Horatio, Marcellus and Barnardo.

HORATIO
Hail to your lordship!

HAMLET
I am glad to see you well.
Horatio—or I've forgotten myself.

HORATIO
The same, my lord,
and your poor servant always.

HAMLET
Sir, my good friend—
I'll trade that name with you.
And what brings you from Wittenberg, Horatio?—
Marcellus?

MARCELLUS
My good lord.

HAMLET
I'm very glad to see you.—Good evening, sir.—
But really, what brings you from Wittenberg?

HORATIO
A truant's mood, my good lord.

HAMLET
I wouldn't let your enemy say that;
nor shall you do my ear that violence
of making it believe your own report
against yourself. I know you are no truant.
But what's your business here in Elsinore?
We'll teach you to drink deep before you leave.

HORATIO
My lord, I came to see your father's funeral.

HAMLET
Please don't mock me, fellow student.
I think it was to see my mother's wedding.

HORATIO
Indeed, my lord, it followed close upon it.

HAMLET
Thrift, thrift, Horatio! The funeral's baked meats
were served up cold for the marriage tables.
I'd rather have met my worst enemy in heaven
than ever have seen that day, Horatio.
My father—I think I see my father.

HORATIO
Where, my lord?

HAMLET
In my mind's eye, Horatio.

HORATIO
I saw him once; he was a fine king.

HAMLET
He was a man, take him for all in all,
I shall not look upon his like again.

HORATIO
My lord, I think I saw him last night.

HAMLET
Saw? Who?

HORATIO
My lord, the King your father.

HAMLET
The King my father!

HORATIO
Calm your astonishment a while,
with an attentive ear, until I can deliver,
on the witness of these gentlemen,
this marvel to you.

HAMLET
For God's love, let me hear.

HORATIO
For two nights running, these gentlemen,
Marcellus and Barnardo, on their watch,
in the dead, vacant middle of the night,
had this encounter. A figure like your father,
armed at every point exactly, head to foot,
appears before them, and with solemn march
goes slow and stately by them. Three times he walked
before their oppressed and fear-struck eyes,
within his baton's length, while they, dissolved
almost to jelly by the act of fear,
stand dumb, and do not speak to him. This, to me,
in dreadful secrecy they confided;
and I, with them, the third night kept the watch,
where, just as they'd reported—both in time,
and in the form of the thing, each word made true—
the apparition comes. I knew your father:
these hands are not more alike.

HAMLET
But where was this?

MARCELLUS
My lord, upon the platform where we watch.

HAMLET
Did you not speak to it?

HORATIO
My lord, I did;
but it made no answer. Yet once I thought
it lifted up its head, and began
to move, as if it would speak.
But just then the morning cock crowed loud,
and at the sound it shrank away in haste
and vanished from our sight.

HAMLET
It's very strange.

HORATIO
As I live, my honored lord, it's true;
and we thought it set down in our duty
to let you know of it.

HAMLET
Indeed, indeed, sirs, but this troubles me.
Do you hold the watch tonight?

MARCELLUS and BARNARDO
We do, my lord.

HAMLET
Armed, you say?

BOTH
Armed, my lord.

HAMLET
From top to toe?

BOTH
My lord, from head to foot.

HAMLET
Then you didn't see his face?

HORATIO
Oh yes, my lord. He wore his visor up.

HAMLET
What, did he look angry?

HORATIO
A countenance more in sorrow than in anger.

HAMLET
Pale, or red?

HORATIO
No, very pale.

HAMLET
And fixed his eyes on you?

HORATIO
Most constantly.

HAMLET
I wish I had been there.

HORATIO
It would have amazed you.

HAMLET
Very likely, very likely. Did it stay long?

HORATIO
Long as one might count to a hundred, at a moderate pace.

MARCELLUS and BARNARDO
Longer, longer.

HORATIO
Not when I saw it.

HAMLET
His beard was grizzled, was it not?

HORATIO
It was, as I have seen it in his life,
a sable touched with silver.

HAMLET
I will watch tonight.
Perhaps it will walk again.

HORATIO
I guarantee it will.

HAMLET
If it takes on my noble father's form,
I'll speak to it, though hell itself should gape
and bid me hold my peace. I beg you all—
if you have until now concealed this sight,
keep it locked still in your silence;
and whatever else may happen tonight,
give it understanding, but no tongue.
I will repay your loves. So, fare you well.
Upon the platform, between eleven and twelve,
I'll visit you.

ALL
Our duty to your honor.

HAMLET
Your love, as mine to you. Farewell.
[_Exeunt Horatio, Marcellus and Barnardo._]

HAMLET
My father's spirit in arms! All is not well.
I suspect some foul play. Would the night were here!
Till then sit still, my soul. Foul deeds will rise,
though all the earth should bury them, to men's eyes.
[_Exit._]
SCENE III. A room in Polonius's house.
Enter Laertes and Ophelia.

LAERTES
My gear is aboard. Farewell.
And, sister, whenever the winds are favorable
and a ship is bound your way, do not sleep,
but let me hear from you.

OPHELIA
Do you doubt that?

LAERTES
As for Hamlet, and the trifle of his attention,
treat it as a passing fancy, a whim of the blood—
a violet in the springtime of youth,
early, not lasting; sweet, but not enduring;
the fragrance and diversion of a minute;
no more.

OPHELIA
No more than that?

LAERTES
Think it no more.
For as nature grows, it grows not only
in muscle and bulk; but as this temple grows,
the inward work of the mind and soul
grows broad with it. Perhaps he loves you now,
and no stain or deceit now sullies
the purity of his intent; but you must fear—
weighing his rank—his will is not his own,
for he himself is subject to his birth.
He may not, as common persons do,
carve his own portion; for on his choice depends
the safety and the health of this whole state;
and therefore his choice must be confined
to the voice and consent of that body
whose head he is. So if he says he loves you,
it suits your wisdom to believe it only
so far as he, in his particular rank and place,
can match his words with deeds; which is no further
than the main voice of Denmark will allow.
Then weigh what your honor stands to lose
if, with too trusting an ear, you take his songs,
or lose your heart, or open your chaste treasure
to his uncurbed insistence.
Fear it, Ophelia; fear it, my dear sister;
and keep yourself behind your affection,
out of the reach and danger of desire.
The most careful girl is reckless enough
if she unveils her beauty to the moon.
Virtue itself does not escape slander's blows.
The cankerworm bites the buds of spring
too often before they even open;
and in the morning, the fresh dew of youth,
contagious blights are most threatening.
Be wary, then: the best safety lies in fear.
Youth rebels against itself, with no one near.

OPHELIA
I'll keep the meaning of this good lesson
as a guard upon my heart. But, good my brother,
don't, like some ungodly preachers do,
show me the steep and thorny way to heaven
while you yourself, a reckless, swollen libertine,
tread the primrose path of pleasure
and pay no heed to your own advice.

LAERTES
Oh, fear not for me.
I stay too long. But here my father comes.
Enter Polonius.

POLONIUS
Still here, Laertes? Aboard, aboard, for shame!
The wind sits in the shoulder of your sail,
and they are waiting for you. There—my blessing on you.
[_Laying his hand on Laertes's head._]

POLONIUS
And these few precepts—in your memory
see that you write them. Give your thoughts no tongue,
nor any rash thought any action.
Be friendly, but by no means common.
Those friends you have, and whose loyalty you've tested,
bind them to your soul with hoops of steel;
but don't wear out your palm with greeting
every new-hatched, half-grown comrade. Beware
of getting into a quarrel; but once in,
bear it so that your opponent learns to fear you.
Give every man your ear, but few your voice;
take each man's opinion, but reserve your judgment.
Let your clothes be costly as your purse can buy,
but not showy; rich, not gaudy—
for the apparel oft proclaims the man,
and those in France of the best rank and station
are most refined and generous in just that.
Neither a borrower nor a lender be,
for a loan often loses both itself and the friend,
and borrowing dulls the edge of thrift.
This above all: to thine own self be true,
and it must follow, as the night the day,
you cannot then be false to any man.
Farewell; may my blessing ripen this in you.

LAERTES
Most humbly do I take my leave, my lord.

POLONIUS
The time invites you; go, your servants wait.

LAERTES
Farewell, Ophelia, and remember well
what I have said to you.

OPHELIA
It's locked within my memory,
and you yourself shall keep the key of it.

LAERTES
Farewell.
[_Exit._]

POLONIUS
What is it, Ophelia, that he said to you?

OPHELIA
If you please—something concerning the Lord Hamlet.

POLONIUS
Well thought of, indeed.
I'm told that he has, very often lately,
given private time to you; and you yourself
have been most free and generous with your company.
If this is so—as it's been reported to me,
and that by way of warning—I must tell you,
you don't understand yourself as clearly
as befits my daughter and your honor.
What is between you? Give me up the truth.

OPHELIA
He has, my lord, of late made many tenders
of his affection to me.

POLONIUS
Affection! Pah! You talk like a green girl,
untested in such perilous circumstances.
Do you believe his tenders, as you call them?

OPHELIA
I do not know, my lord, what I should think.

POLONIUS
Well, I'll teach you. Think yourself a baby,
that you have taken these tenders for true coin,
which are not sterling. Tender yourself more dearly—
or (not to wear out the poor word,
running it like this) you'll tender me a fool.

OPHELIA
My lord, he has pressed his love on me
in honorable fashion.

POLONIUS
Ay, fashion, you may call it. Come, come.

OPHELIA
And has backed up his words, my lord,
with almost all the holy vows of heaven.

POLONIUS
Ay—snares to catch foolish birds. I know well,
when the blood is burning, how freely the soul
lends the tongue its vows. These flares, daughter,
giving more light than heat, going out in both,
even as they're promised, in the very making,
you must not mistake for fire. From this time on,
be somewhat more sparing of your company.
Set your conversation at a higher price
than a mere command to talk. As for Lord Hamlet,
believe only this much in him: that he is young,
and may walk on a longer leash
than can be granted you. In short, Ophelia,
don't believe his vows; for they are go-betweens,
not of the color that their garments show,
but mere petitioners for unholy ends,
breathing like holy and pious pimps,
the better to deceive. This is the sum:
in plain terms, from this time forward
I'll not have you so slander any moment's leisure
as to give words or talk with the Lord Hamlet.
See to it, I command you. Come along.

OPHELIA
I shall obey, my lord.
[_Exeunt._]
SCENE IV. The platform.
Enter Hamlet, Horatio and Marcellus.

HAMLET
The air bites sharply; it is very cold.

HORATIO
It is a nipping and a biting air.

HAMLET
What hour now?

HORATIO
Not quite twelve, I think.

MARCELLUS
No, it has struck.

HORATIO
Really? I didn't hear it. Then it draws near the time
when the spirit usually walks.
[_A flourish of trumpets, and ordnance shot off within._]

HORATIO
What does this mean, my lord?

HAMLET
The King is up tonight, and carousing,
holding his revels, the staggering dance reeling;
and as he drains his cups of Rhine wine down,
the kettle-drum and trumpet bray out
the triumph of his toast.

HORATIO
Is it a custom?

HAMLET
Ay, indeed it is;
and to my mind, though I'm a native here
and to the manner born, it is a custom
more honored in the breach than the observance.
This heavy-headed drinking, east and west,
makes us slandered and condemned by other nations.
They call us drunkards, and with filthy words
stain our reputation; and indeed it strips
from our achievements—even at their best—
the very heart and substance of our good name.
So it often happens with particular men
that, for some single flaw of nature in them—
as in their birth, in which they have no guilt,
since nature cannot choose its own origin—
by the overgrowth of some one temperament,
often breaking down the fences and forts of reason,
or by some habit that too much corrupts
the form of pleasing manners—that these men,
carrying, I say, the stamp of one defect,
whether nature's marking or fortune's mark,
their other virtues, be they pure as grace,
as infinite as any man may have,
shall, in the general judgment, take corruption
from that one particular fault. The dram of evil
does drag down all the noble substance
to its own disgrace.

HORATIO
Look, my lord, it comes!
Enter Ghost.

HAMLET
Angels and ministers of grace defend us!
Whether you are a spirit of health or a goblin damned,
whether you bring airs from heaven or blasts from hell,
whether your intentions are wicked or kind,
you come in such a questionable shape
that I will speak to you. I'll call you Hamlet,
King, father, royal Dane. Oh, answer me!
Let me not burst with ignorance; but tell me
why your sanctified bones, sealed up in death,
have burst their burial shroud; why the tomb,
in which we saw you quietly laid to rest,
has opened its heavy marble jaws
to cast you up again. What can it mean,
that you, dead corpse, again in full armor,
revisit thus the glimpses of the moon,
making the night hideous, and we, fools of nature,
so horribly shake our composure
with thoughts beyond the reach of our souls?
Say, why is this? Why? What should we do?
[_Ghost beckons Hamlet._]

HORATIO
It beckons you to go away with it,
as if it wished to make some communication
to you alone.

MARCELLUS
Look with what courteous action
it waves you to a more secluded ground.
But do not go with it.

HORATIO
No, by no means.

HAMLET
It will not speak; then I will follow it.

HORATIO
Do not, my lord.

HAMLET
Why, what is there to fear?
I do not value my life at a pin's worth;
and as for my soul, what can it do to that,
being a thing immortal as itself?
It waves me forward again. I'll follow it.

HORATIO
What if it tempts you toward the flood, my lord,
or to the dreadful summit of the cliff
that overhangs its base into the sea,
and there takes on some other horrible form
that might strip your reason of its rule
and draw you into madness? Think of it.
The very place breeds desperate fancies
in every brain, with no other cause,
that looks down so many fathoms to the sea
and hears it roar below.

HAMLET
It waves me still.
Go on, I'll follow you.

MARCELLUS
You shall not go, my lord.

HAMLET
Hold off your hands.

HORATIO
Be ruled; you shall not go.

HAMLET
My fate cries out,
and makes each tiny artery in this body
as tough as the Nemean lion's sinew.
[_Ghost beckons._]

HAMLET
Still it calls me. Let go of me, gentlemen.
[_Breaking free from them._]

HAMLET
By heaven, I'll make a ghost of anyone who stops me.
I say, away!—Go on, I'll follow you.
[_Exeunt Ghost and Hamlet._]

HORATIO
He grows desperate with imagination.

MARCELLUS
Let's follow. It's not right to obey him in this.

HORATIO
Let's go after him. What will this come to?

MARCELLUS
Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.

HORATIO
Heaven will direct it.

MARCELLUS
No, let's follow him.
[_Exeunt._]
SCENE V. A more remote part of the Castle.
Enter Ghost and Hamlet.

HAMLET
Where will you lead me? Speak. I'll go no further.

GHOST
Mark me.

HAMLET
I will.

GHOST
My hour is almost come,
when I to sulfurous and tormenting flames
must render up myself.

HAMLET
Alas, poor ghost!

GHOST
Do not pity me, but lend your serious hearing
to what I shall reveal.

HAMLET
Speak. I am bound to hear.

GHOST
So are you bound to revenge, when you shall hear.

HAMLET
What?

GHOST
I am your father's spirit,
doomed for a certain term to walk the night,
and by day confined to fast in fires,
till the foul crimes done in my lifetime
are burnt and purged away. But that I am forbidden
to tell the secrets of my prison house,
I could unfold a tale whose lightest word
would harrow up your soul, freeze your young blood,
make your two eyes, like stars, start from their orbits,
your knotted and combined locks part,
and each particular hair to stand on end
like quills upon the bristling porcupine.
But this revelation of eternity must not be
for ears of flesh and blood. Listen, listen, oh, listen!
If you did ever love your dear father—

HAMLET
O God!

GHOST
Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder.

HAMLET
Murder!

HAMLET
Haste me to know it, so that I, with wings as swift
as meditation or the thoughts of love,
may sweep to my revenge.

GHOST
I find you ready;
and you would be duller than the bloated weed
that rots itself in ease on Lethe's shore
if you would not stir at this. Now, Hamlet, hear.
The story given out is that, sleeping in my orchard,
a serpent stung me; so the whole ear of Denmark
is, by a faked account of my death,
grossly deceived. But know, you noble youth,
the serpent that did sting your father's life
now wears his crown.

HAMLET
O my prophetic soul!
My uncle!

GHOST
Ay, that incestuous, that adulterous beast,
with the witchcraft of his wit, with traitorous gifts—
oh, wicked wit, and gifts, that have the power
so to seduce!—won to his shameful lust
the will of my most seemingly virtuous queen.
O Hamlet, what a falling-off was there!
From me, whose love was of that dignity
that it went hand in hand even with the vow
I made to her in marriage; and to sink down
to a wretch whose natural gifts were poor
beside my own. But just as virtue is never moved,
though lewdness courts it in the shape of heaven,
so lust, though linked to a radiant angel,
will gorge itself in a heavenly bed
and feed on garbage.
But wait! I think I scent the morning air.
Let me be brief. Sleeping within my orchard,
as was always my custom in the afternoon,
in my unguarded hour your uncle stole upon me
with the juice of cursed henbane in a vial,
and in the porches of my ears he poured
the leprous distillation, whose effect
holds such an enmity with the blood of man
that, swift as quicksilver, it courses through
the natural gates and alleys of the body,
and with a sudden force it clots and curdles,
like sour drops dripped into milk,
the thin and wholesome blood. So it did mine;
and instantly a scabbing crust spread over,
most leper-like, with vile and loathsome scab,
all my smooth body.
Thus was I, sleeping, by a brother's hand,
of life, of crown, of queen at once cut off;
struck down in the full blossom of my sins,
with no last rites, no sacrament, no anointing;
no final reckoning made, but sent to my account
with all my imperfections on my head.
O horrible! O horrible! most horrible!
If you have any natural feeling in you, do not bear it;
let not the royal bed of Denmark be
a couch for lust and damnèd incest.
But however you pursue this act,
do not taint your mind, nor let your soul plot
anything against your mother; leave her to heaven,
and to those thorns that lodge within her breast
to prick and sting her. Fare you well at once!
The glow-worm shows the morning to be near,
and begins to dim his feeble fire.
Adieu, adieu, adieu. Remember me.
[_Exit._]

HAMLET
O all you host of heaven! O earth! What else?
And shall I add hell too? Oh, no! Hold, my heart;
and you, my sinews, do not grow old in an instant,
but bear me stiffly up. Remember you?
Ay, you poor ghost, while memory holds a seat
in this distracted globe. Remember you?
Yes—from the tablet of my memory
I'll wipe away all trivial, foolish records,
all sayings from books, all forms, all impressions past
that youth and observation copied there;
and your commandment, all alone, shall live
within the book and volume of my brain,
unmixed with baser matter. Yes, by heaven!
O most pernicious woman!
O villain, villain, smiling, damnèd villain!
My notebook. It's only right that I set it down,
that a man may smile, and smile, and be a villain—
at least I'm sure it may be so in Denmark.
[_Writing._]

HAMLET
So, uncle, there you are. Now to my watchword:
it is "Adieu, adieu, remember me."
I have sworn it.

HORATIO and MARCELLUS
[_Within._] My lord, my lord!

MARCELLUS
[_Within._] Lord Hamlet!

HORATIO
[_Within._] Heaven keep him safe.

HAMLET
So be it!

MARCELLUS
[_Within._] Hey, ho, ho, my lord!

HAMLET
Hey, ho, ho, boy! Come, bird, come.
Enter Horatio and Marcellus.

MARCELLUS
How is it, my noble lord?

HORATIO
What news, my lord?

HAMLET
Oh, wonderful!

HORATIO
Good my lord, tell it.

HAMLET
No, you'll reveal it.

HORATIO
Not I, my lord, by heaven.

MARCELLUS
Nor I, my lord.

HAMLET
How say you, then—would the heart of man ever think it?—
but you'll keep it secret?

HORATIO and MARCELLUS
Ay, by heaven, my lord.

HAMLET
There's not a villain living in all Denmark
but he's a thorough scoundrel.

HORATIO
There's no need for a ghost, my lord, to come from the grave
to tell us this.

HAMLET
Why, right; you're in the right;
and so, without any more ado,
I think it fitting that we shake hands and part:
you, where your business and desire shall point you—
for every man has business and desire,
such as it is—and for my own poor part,
look you, I'll go pray.

HORATIO
These are but wild and whirling words, my lord.

HORATIO
There's no offense, my lord.

HAMLET
Yes, by Saint Patrick, but there is, Horatio,
and much offense too. As for this vision here—
it is an honest ghost, that I can tell you.
As for your desire to know what's between us,
master it as best you can. And now, good friends,
as you are friends, scholars, and soldiers,
grant me one poor request.

HORATIO
What is it, my lord? We will.

HAMLET
Never make known what you have seen tonight.

HORATIO and MARCELLUS
My lord, we will not.

HAMLET
No, but swear it.

HORATIO
In faith, my lord, not I.

MARCELLUS
Nor I, my lord, in faith.

HAMLET
Upon my sword.

MARCELLUS
We have sworn already, my lord.

HAMLET
Indeed, upon my sword, indeed.

GHOST
[_Cries under the stage._] Swear.

HAMLET
Ha, ha, boy! Is that what you say? Are you there, trusty fellow?
Come on—you hear this fellow in the cellar.
Consent to swear.

HORATIO
Propose the oath, my lord.

HAMLET
Never to speak of what you have seen.
Swear by my sword.

GHOST
[_Beneath._] Swear.

HAMLET
_Hic et ubique?_ Then we'll shift our ground.
Come over here, gentlemen,
and lay your hands again upon my sword.
Never to speak of what you have heard.
Swear by my sword.

GHOST
[_Beneath._] Swear.

HAMLET
Well said, old mole! Can you work in the earth so fast?
A fine sapper! Once more move, good friends.

HORATIO
O day and night, but this is wondrous strange.

HAMLET
And therefore, as a stranger, give it welcome.
There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio,
than are dreamt of in your philosophy. But come—
here, as before, swear: never, so help you mercy,
however strange or odd I bear myself
(since I may think it fitting, hereafter,
to put an antic disposition on),
that you, at such times, seeing me, shall never,
with arms folded thus, or with this shake of the head,
or by the uttering of some doubtful phrase
like "Well, we know," or "We could, if we would,"
or "If we cared to speak," or "There are those who could, if they might"—
or any such ambiguous hint—to show
that you know anything of me. This you must not do—
so grace and mercy at your hour of greatest need help you.
Swear.

GHOST
[_Beneath._] Swear.

HAMLET
Rest, rest, perturbed spirit. So, gentlemen,
with all my love I commend myself to you;
and whatever so poor a man as Hamlet is
may do to express his love and friendship to you,
God willing, shall not be lacking. Let us go in together;
and keep your fingers on your lips, I beg you.
The time is out of joint. O cursèd spite,
that ever I was born to set it right!
No, come, let's go together.
[_Exeunt._]

paragraphs: SCENE I. A room in Polonius's house.
Enter Polonius and Reynaldo.

POLONIUS
Give him this money and these notes, Reynaldo.

REYNALDO
I will, my lord.

POLONIUS
You'll do marvelously wisely, good Reynaldo,
to make some inquiry about his behavior
before you visit him.

REYNALDO
My lord, I did intend to.

POLONIUS
Well said—very well said. Look here, sir:
first ask what Danes there are in Paris,
and how, and who, what means they have, and where they lodge,
what company they keep, at what expense; and finding,
by this roundabout drift of questions,
that they do know my son, then close in nearer
than your direct questions would reach.
Let on that you have some distant knowledge of him—
as thus: "I know his father and his friends,
and, in part, him." Do you follow this, Reynaldo?

REYNALDO
Ay, very well, my lord.

POLONIUS
"And, in part, him—but," you may say, "not well;
but if it's the one I mean, he's very wild,
addicted to this and that"—and then pin on him
whatever lies you please. Nothing so vile, mind,
as would dishonor him—take care of that—
but, sir, such loose, wild, everyday slips
as are the well-known companions
of youth and freedom.

REYNALDO
Like gambling, my lord?

POLONIUS
Ay, or drinking, fencing, swearing,
quarreling, whoring—you may go that far.

REYNALDO
My lord, that would dishonor him.

POLONIUS
No, honestly—not if you season the charge right.
You must not lay another scandal on him,
that he's given to outright debauchery;
that's not my meaning. Breathe out his faults so deftly
that they seem only the blemishes of freedom,
the flash and outburst of a fiery mind,
a wildness in unbroken blood,
that strikes at all young men.

REYNALDO
But, my good lord—

POLONIUS
Why should you do this?

REYNALDO
Ay, my lord, I'd like to know that.

POLONIUS
Well, sir, here's my aim,
and I believe it's a trick that works.
When you've laid these slight stains on my son,
as though he were a thing a little soiled in the handling—
mark me—
your man in conversation, the one you'd sound out,
if he has ever seen the youth you describe
guilty of the crimes you named, rest assured
he'll fall in with you, like this:
"Good sir," or so; or "friend," or "gentleman"—
according to the phrase and the form of address
of his rank and country.

REYNALDO
Very good, my lord.

POLONIUS
And then, sir, he does this—he does—
What was I about to say? By the mass, I was about to say something. Where did I leave off?

REYNALDO
At "he'll fall in with you,"
at "friend or so," and "gentleman."

POLONIUS
At "he'll fall in with you"—ay, indeed!
He falls in with you like this: "I know the gentleman.
I saw him yesterday, or the other day,
or then, or then, with such and such; and, as you say,
there he was gambling; there he was overtaken in his drink;
there quarreling at tennis"—or perhaps,
"I saw him go into such a house of ill repute"—
that is, a brothel, or the like. You see now,
your bait of falsehood catches this carp of truth;
and so we men of wisdom and far reach,
with roundabout casts and sidelong feints,
by indirections find directions out.
So, by my lesson and advice just now,
shall you find out my son. You follow me, don't you?

REYNALDO
My lord, I do.

POLONIUS
God be with you. Fare you well.

REYNALDO
Good my lord.

POLONIUS
Study his leanings for yourself.

REYNALDO
I shall, my lord.

POLONIUS
And let him keep up his music.

REYNALDO
Well, my lord.

POLONIUS
Farewell.
[_Exit Reynaldo._]
Enter Ophelia.

POLONIUS
What now, Ophelia—what's the matter?

OPHELIA
Oh, my lord, I have been so frightened.

POLONIUS
By what, in the name of God?

OPHELIA
My lord, as I was sewing in my room,
Lord Hamlet—his jacket all unfastened,
no hat upon his head, his stockings dirty,
ungartered, and fallen down around his ankles,
pale as his shirt, his knees knocking together,
and with a look so pitiful in its meaning
as if he had been let loose out of hell
to tell of horrors—he comes before me.

POLONIUS
Mad for love of you?

OPHELIA
My lord, I do not know, but truly I do fear it.

POLONIUS
What did he say?

OPHELIA
He took me by the wrist and held me hard;
then draws back to the full length of his arm,
and with his other hand held thus above his brow,
he falls to studying my face so closely
as though he'd draw it. Long he stayed like that.
At last—a little shaking of my arm,
and three times nodding his head up and down—
he raised a sigh so pitiful and deep
it seemed to shatter his whole frame
and end his life. That done, he lets me go,
and, with his head turned back over his shoulder,
he seemed to find his way without his eyes,
for out the door he went without their help,
and to the last kept their light fixed on me.

POLONIUS
Come, go with me. I'll go and find the King.
This is the very madness of love,
whose violent nature destroys itself
and drives the will to desperate undertakings,
as often as any passion under heaven
that afflicts our nature. I am sorry—
what, have you given him any hard words lately?

OPHELIA
No, my good lord; but, as you did command,
I refused his letters and denied
his access to me.

POLONIUS
That has made him mad.
I'm sorry that I didn't watch him
with better care and judgment. I feared he was only toying with you,
and meant to ruin you. But curse my suspicion!
It seems it's as natural to us old men
to overshoot in our suspicions
as it is common for the younger sort
to lack all caution. Come, let's go to the King.
This must be known; kept quiet, it might breed
more grief by hiding than hate by telling this love.
[_Exeunt._]
SCENE II. A room in the Castle.
Enter King, Queen, Rosencrantz, Guildenstern and Attendants.

KING
Welcome, dear Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.
Besides our great longing to see you,
the need we have to make use of you spurred
our hasty summons. You've heard something
of Hamlet's transformation—so I call it,
since neither the outer nor the inner man
resembles what it was. What it could be,
beyond his father's death, that has so put him
beside the understanding of himself,
I cannot guess. I beg you both,
since you were brought up with him from such young days,
and are so close in age and temperament,
to stay here at our court awhile,
so that your company may draw him out
to pleasures, and may gather, as occasion lets you,
whether anything unknown to us afflicts him
that, once revealed, lies within our cure.

QUEEN
Good gentlemen, he has talked much of you,
and I am sure there are not two men living
to whom he's more attached. If it would please you
to show us so much grace and good will
as to spend some time with us awhile,
for the help and furtherance of our hope,
your visit shall receive such thanks
as suit a king's remembering.

ROSENCRANTZ
Both your majesties
might, by the sovereign power you have over us,
lay your dread wishes on us as commands
rather than requests.

GUILDENSTERN
We both obey,
and here give ourselves up, to the full,
to lay our service freely at your feet,
to be commanded.

KING
Thanks, Rosencrantz and gentle Guildenstern.

QUEEN
Thanks, Guildenstern and gentle Rosencrantz.
And I beg you, go at once and visit
my too-much-changed son. Go, some of you,
and bring these gentlemen to where Hamlet is.

GUILDENSTERN
May heaven make our presence and our efforts
pleasant and helpful to him.

QUEEN
Ay, amen.
[_Exeunt Rosencrantz, Guildenstern and some Attendants._]
Enter Polonius.

POLONIUS
The ambassadors from Norway, my good lord,
are back, and joyfully.

KING
You have always been the father of good news.

POLONIUS
Have I, my lord? I assure you, my good liege,
I hold my duty, as I hold my soul,
both to my God and to my gracious King;
and I do think—or else this brain of mine
no longer hunts the trail of statecraft as surely
as it once did—that I have found
the very cause of Hamlet's madness.

KING
Oh, speak of that—that I long to hear.

POLONIUS
Give the ambassadors their hearing first.
My news shall be the dessert to that great feast.

KING
Do them the honor yourself, and bring them in.
[_Exit Polonius._]

KING
He tells me, my sweet queen, that he has found
the head and source of all your son's distress.

QUEEN
I doubt it's anything but the obvious thing—
his father's death and our too-hasty marriage.

KING
Well, we shall sound him out.
Enter Polonius with Voltemand and Cornelius.

KING
Welcome, my good friends!
Say, Voltemand, what news from our brother of Norway?

VOLTEMAND
The fairest return of greetings and goodwill.
Upon our first word, he sent to suppress
his nephew's troop levies, which he had thought
were a preparation against Poland;
but, looking closer, he truly found
it was against your Highness. Grieved at this—
that his own sickness, age, and helplessness
had been so abused—he sends out orders
arresting Fortinbras; who, in short, obeys,
takes a rebuke from Norway, and in the end
vows before his uncle never again
to try force of arms against your Majesty.
At which old Norway, overcome with joy,
gives him three thousand crowns a year,
and his commission to employ those soldiers,
so levied as before, against the Poles;
with a request, set out more fully here—
[_Gives a paper._]
that it might please you to grant safe passage
through your domains for this campaign,
on such terms of safety and allowance
as are written down inside.

KING
It pleases us well;
and at a more considered time we'll read,
answer, and think upon this business.
Meanwhile, we thank you for your good labor.
Go, take your rest. Tonight we'll feast together.
Most welcome home.
[_Exeunt Voltemand and Cornelius._]

POLONIUS
This business is well ended.
My liege and madam, to hold forth on
what majesty should be, what duty is,
why day is day, night night, and time is time,
would be only to waste night, day, and time.
Therefore, since brevity is the soul of wit,
and tediousness is the limbs and outward show,
I will be brief. Your noble son is mad.
Mad I call it; for, to define true madness,
what is it but to be nothing else but mad?
But let that go.

QUEEN
More matter, with less art.

POLONIUS
Madam, I swear I use no art at all.
That he is mad, it's true; it's true it's a pity;
and it's a pity it's true—a foolish turn of phrase,
but goodbye to it, for I will use no art.
Mad let us grant him, then. And now it remains
that we find out the cause of this effect—
or rather say, the cause of this defect,
for this defective effect comes from a cause.
Thus it stands, and the rest stands thus. Consider:
I have a daughter—have, while she is mine—
who, in her duty and obedience, mark,
has given me this. Now hear it, and judge.
[_Reads._]
"To the heavenly, and my soul's idol, the most beautified Ophelia"—
that's an ugly phrase, a vile phrase; "beautified" is a vile phrase—but you shall hear. Then:
[_Reads._]
"these; in her excellent white bosom, these," and so on.

QUEEN
Did this come from Hamlet to her?

POLONIUS
Good madam, wait awhile; I will be exact.
[_Reads._]
"Doubt that the stars are fire,
doubt that the sun does move,
doubt truth to be a liar,
but never doubt I love.
O dear Ophelia, I am bad at this verse. I have no skill to count out my groans. But that I love you best, oh, best of all, believe it. Goodbye.
Yours forever, most dear lady, as long as this body is his,
HAMLET."
This, in obedience, my daughter has shown me;
and more than that, she has told me all his courting—
as it fell out, by time, by means, and place—
laid every word in my ear.

KING
But how has she received his love?

POLONIUS
What do you think of me?

KING
As of a man faithful and honorable.

POLONIUS
I'd gladly prove so. But what might you think,
when I had seen this hot love taking wing—
as I noticed it, I must tell you, before
my daughter told me—what might you,
or my dear Majesty, your queen here, think,
if I had played the writing-desk or notebook,
or winked at my own heart, gone mute and dumb,
or looked upon this love with idle eyes—
what might you think? No, I went straight to work,
and to my young lady I said this:
"Lord Hamlet is a prince, out of your sphere;
this must not be." And then I gave her orders
that she should shut herself off from his visits,
admit no messengers, take in no gifts.
Which done, she took the fruits of my advice;
and he, rebuffed—to make the tale short—
fell into a sadness, then into a fast,
then to a sleeplessness, then to a weakness,
then to a lightheadedness, and, by this decline,
into the madness he now raves in,
which all of us mourn.

KING
Do you think it's this?

QUEEN
It may be; very likely.

POLONIUS
Has there ever been a time—I'd dearly like to know—
when I have positively said "It is so,"
and it proved otherwise?

KING
Not that I know.

POLONIUS
Take this from this, if it's otherwise.
[_Points to his head and shoulder._]
If circumstances lead me, I will find
where truth is hidden, though it were hidden
at the center of the earth.

KING
How can we test it further?

POLONIUS
You know, sometimes he walks for hours together
here in the lobby.

QUEEN
So he does indeed.

POLONIUS
At such a time, I'll loose my daughter to him.
You and I will be behind a curtain then;
watch the encounter. If he doesn't love her,
and hasn't lost his reason over it,
let me be no royal counselor,
but keep a farm and farmhands.

KING
We'll try it.
Enter Hamlet, reading.

QUEEN
But look where the poor wretch comes, reading, so sadly.

POLONIUS
Away, I beg you, both of you, away.
I'll go at him right now. Oh, give me leave.
[_Exeunt King, Queen and Attendants._]

POLONIUS
How is my good Lord Hamlet?

HAMLET
Well, thank God.

POLONIUS
Do you know me, my lord?

HAMLET
Very well. You're a fishmonger.

POLONIUS
Not I, my lord.

HAMLET
Then I wish you were as honest a man.

POLONIUS
Honest, my lord?

HAMLET
Ay, sir; to be honest, the way this world goes, is to be one man picked out of ten thousand.

POLONIUS
That's very true, my lord.

HAMLET
For if the sun breeds maggots in a dead dog—a carcass good enough for the sun to kiss—
Have you a daughter?

POLONIUS
I have, my lord.

HAMLET
Don't let her walk in the sun. Conception is a blessing, but not the kind your daughter might come by. Friend, see to it.

POLONIUS
[_Aside._] What do you make of that? Still harping on my daughter. And yet he didn't know me at first; he said I was a fishmonger. He's far gone, far gone. And truly, in my youth I suffered great extremes for love—very near this. I'll speak to him again.—What are you reading, my lord?

HAMLET
Words, words, words.

POLONIUS
What is the matter, my lord?

HAMLET
Between whom?

POLONIUS
I mean the matter that you read, my lord.

HAMLET
Slanders, sir. For this satirical rogue says here that old men have gray beards; that their faces are wrinkled; that their eyes ooze thick amber and gum from a plum tree; and that they have a plentiful lack of wit, together with very weak legs. All of which, sir, though I most powerfully and forcibly believe, still I don't think it decent to set it down like this. For you yourself, sir, would be as old as I am—if, like a crab, you could go backward.

POLONIUS
[_Aside._] Though this be madness, yet there is method in it.—Will you step out of the open air, my lord?

HAMLET
Into my grave?

POLONIUS
Indeed, that's out of the air. [_Aside._] How telling his replies sometimes are! A luck that madness often hits on, which reason and sanity couldn't so happily give birth to. I'll leave him, and at once contrive a way to bring him and my daughter together.—My honorable lord, I'll most humbly take my leave of you.

HAMLET
You cannot, sir, take anything from me that I'll more willingly part with—except my life, except my life, except my life.

POLONIUS
Fare you well, my lord.

HAMLET
These tedious old fools.
Enter Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

POLONIUS
You go to find Lord Hamlet; there he is.

ROSENCRANTZ
[_To Polonius._] God save you, sir.
[_Exit Polonius._]

GUILDENSTERN
My honored lord!

ROSENCRANTZ
My most dear lord!

HAMLET
My excellent good friends! How are you, Guildenstern? Ah, Rosencrantz. Good lads, how are you both?

ROSENCRANTZ
Like the ordinary children of the earth.

HAMLET
Nor the soles of her shoe?

ROSENCRANTZ
Neither, my lord.

HAMLET
Then you live around her waist, or in the middle of her favors?

GUILDENSTERN
Honestly, we're her privates.

HAMLET
In the secret parts of Fortune? Oh, very true; she's a whore. What's the news?

ROSENCRANTZ
None, my lord, except that the world's grown honest.

HAMLET
Then doomsday's near. But your news isn't true. Let me question you more particularly. What have you, my good friends, done to deserve, at the hands of Fortune, that she sends you here to prison?

GUILDENSTERN
Prison, my lord?

HAMLET
Denmark's a prison.

ROSENCRANTZ
Then the whole world is one.

HAMLET
A fine one, in which there are many cells, wards, and dungeons—Denmark being one of the worst.

ROSENCRANTZ
We don't think so, my lord.

HAMLET
Why, then it's none to you; for there's nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so. To me it is a prison.

ROSENCRANTZ
Why, then your ambition makes it one; it's too cramped for your mind.

HAMLET
O God, I could be bounded in a nutshell and count myself a king of infinite space—were it not that I have bad dreams.

GUILDENSTERN
Which dreams, indeed, are ambition; for the very substance of the ambitious is merely the shadow of a dream.

HAMLET
A dream itself is only a shadow.

ROSENCRANTZ
True, and I hold ambition to be of so airy and weightless a quality that it's only the shadow of a shadow.

HAMLET
Then our beggars are the real bodies, and our monarchs and grand stretched-out heroes are the beggars' shadows. Shall we go to the court? For, by my faith, I cannot reason.

ROSENCRANTZ and GUILDENSTERN
We'll attend you.

HAMLET
No such thing. I won't lump you in with the rest of my servants; for, to speak to you like an honest man, I am most dreadfully waited on. But, on the plain road of friendship, what are you doing at Elsinore?

ROSENCRANTZ
To visit you, my lord; no other reason.

HAMLET
Beggar that I am, I'm even poor in thanks; but I thank you—and surely, dear friends, my thanks aren't worth a halfpenny. Weren't you sent for? Is it your own inclination? Is it a free visit? Come, deal honestly with me. Come, come—out with it.

GUILDENSTERN
What should we say, my lord?

HAMLET
Why, anything—but to the point. You were sent for; and there's a kind of confession in your faces, which your modesty hasn't the craft to disguise. I know the good King and Queen have sent for you.

ROSENCRANTZ
To what end, my lord?

HAMLET
That you must teach me. But let me appeal to you, by the bonds of our fellowship, by the harmony of our youth, by the duty of our ever-kept love, and by whatever dearer thing a better pleader could press on you—be straight and direct with me: were you sent for, or not?

ROSENCRANTZ
[_To Guildenstern._] What do you say?

HAMLET
[_Aside._] No, then I've got my eye on you.—If you love me, don't hold back.

GUILDENSTERN
My lord, we were sent for.

HAMLET
I'll tell you why; so my guessing will spare you the disclosure, and your secrecy to the King and Queen won't molt a feather. I have, lately—though why I don't know—lost all my mirth, given up all my usual exercises; and indeed it weighs so heavily on my spirit that this goodly frame, the earth, seems to me a sterile promontory; this most excellent canopy, the air—look you—this brave overhanging sky, this majestic roof studded with golden fire—why, it seems to me nothing but a foul and pestilent gathering of vapors. What a piece of work is man! How noble in reason, how infinite in faculties, in form and movement how precise and admirable, in action how like an angel, in understanding how like a god—the beauty of the world, the paragon of animals! And yet, to me, what is this quintessence of dust? Man delights not me—no, nor woman either, though by your smiling you seem to say so.

ROSENCRANTZ
My lord, there was no such thought in my mind.

HAMLET
Why did you laugh, then, when I said "Man delights not me"?

ROSENCRANTZ
To think, my lord, that if man doesn't delight you, what a lean welcome the players will get from you. We passed them on the road; and they're coming here to offer you their service.

HAMLET
The one who plays the king shall be welcome—his Majesty shall have his due from me; the adventurous knight shall use his foil and shield; the lover shall not sigh for free; the comic man shall finish his part in peace; the clown shall make those laugh whose lungs are easily tickled; and the lady shall speak her mind freely, or the blank verse shall limp for it. What players are they?

ROSENCRANTZ
The very ones you used to take such delight in—the tragic actors of the city.

HAMLET
How does it happen they're traveling? Staying put, both in reputation and profit, was better for them every way.

ROSENCRANTZ
I think their ban from the city comes from the recent upheaval.

HAMLET
Do they still stand in the same esteem they did when I was in the city? Are they so popular?

ROSENCRANTZ
No, indeed, they're not.

HAMLET
How's that? Are they growing rusty?

ROSENCRANTZ
No, their effort keeps to its usual pace; but there is, sir, a whole nestful of children, little fledgling hawks, who shriek out their lines at the top of their range and are clapped for it most extravagantly. These are now the fashion, and they so rail at the ordinary stages—so they call them—that many a gentleman wearing a sword is afraid of the playwrights' pens and scarcely dares go there.

HAMLET
What, are they children? Who keeps them? How are they paid? Will they follow the trade no longer than they can sing? Won't they say afterward—if they grow up to be ordinary players, which is most likely, if their means are no better—that their writers wronged them, making them rail against the very career they'll inherit?

ROSENCRANTZ
Honestly, there's been much ado on both sides; and the nation thinks it no sin to egg them on to a quarrel. For a while there, no one would pay for a play unless the playwright and the actor came to blows in it.

HAMLET
Is it possible?

GUILDENSTERN
Oh, there's been a great throwing about of brains.

HAMLET
Do the boys win the day?

ROSENCRANTZ
Ay, that they do, my lord—Hercules and his load too.

HAMLET
It's not so strange; for my uncle is King of Denmark, and those who would have made faces at him while my father lived now give twenty, forty, fifty, a hundred ducats apiece for his portrait in miniature. By God's blood, there is something in this beyond nature, if only philosophy could find it out.
[_Flourish of trumpets within._]

GUILDENSTERN
There are the players.

HAMLET
Gentlemen, you're welcome to Elsinore. Your hands—come. The trappings of a welcome are manners and ceremony. Let me observe them with you, in this style, so that my reception of the players—which, I tell you, must look generous on the surface—won't seem warmer than yours. You're welcome. But my uncle-father and aunt-mother are deceived.

GUILDENSTERN
In what, my dear lord?

HAMLET
I'm only mad north-north-west. When the wind is southerly, I know a hawk from a handsaw.
Enter Polonius.

POLONIUS
Good day to you, gentlemen.

HAMLET
Listen, Guildenstern—and you too—a hearer at each ear: that great baby you see there isn't out of his swaddling clothes yet.

ROSENCRANTZ
Maybe he's come round to them a second time; for they say an old man is twice a child.

HAMLET
I'll prophesy that he comes to tell me about the players. Watch.—You're right, sir; it was indeed Monday morning.

POLONIUS
My lord, I have news to tell you.

HAMLET
My lord, I have news to tell you. When Roscius was an actor in Rome—

POLONIUS
The actors have come here, my lord.

HAMLET
Bah, bah.

POLONIUS
Upon my honor.

HAMLET
Then came each actor on his ass—

POLONIUS
The best actors in the world, whether for tragedy, comedy, history, pastoral, pastoral-comical, historical-pastoral, tragical-historical, tragical-comical-historical-pastoral; for the strictly-plotted scene, or the poem without limits. Seneca can't be too heavy for them, nor Plautus too light. For the written rules and for free improvising, these are the only men.

HAMLET
O Jephthah, judge of Israel, what a treasure you had!

POLONIUS
What treasure did he have, my lord?

HAMLET
Why—
"One fair daughter, and no more,
whom he loved exceedingly well."

POLONIUS
[_Aside._] Still on my daughter.

HAMLET
Am I not right, old Jephthah?

POLONIUS
If you call me Jephthah, my lord, I do have a daughter that I love exceedingly well.

HAMLET
No, that's not what follows.

POLONIUS
What follows, then, my lord?

HAMLET
Why—
"As by lot, God knows,"
and then, you know,
"it came to pass, as most likely it was—"
The first line of the holy ballad will show you the rest. For look where my interruption comes.
Enter four or five Players.

HAMLET
You're welcome, masters; welcome, all.—I'm glad to see you well.—Welcome, good friends.—Oh, my old friend! Your face is fringed with a beard since I saw you last. Have you come to brave me out in Denmark?—What, my young lady and mistress! By our Lady, your ladyship is nearer to heaven than when I saw you last—by the height of a high-heeled shoe. Pray God your voice, like a gold coin gone out of circulation, isn't cracked inside the ring. Masters, you're all welcome. We'll fall to it like French falconers, fly at anything we see. We'll have a speech right now. Come, give us a taste of your quality. Come, a passionate speech.

FIRST PLAYER
What speech, my lord?

HAMLET
I heard you once speak a speech to me—but it was never acted; or, if it was, not more than once, for the play, I remember, didn't please the masses; it was caviar to the common crowd. But it was—as I received it, and others, whose judgment in such matters outranked my own—an excellent play, well laid out in its scenes, set down with as much restraint as skill. I remember someone said there were no spicy bits in the lines to give the matter flavor, nor anything in the phrasing that could convict the author of affectation; but he called it an honest style, as wholesome as it was sweet, and far more handsome than fancy. One speech in it I especially loved—it was Aeneas's tale to Dido, and the part of it especially where he tells of Priam's killing. If it's still alive in your memory, begin at this line—let me see, let me see—
"The rugged Pyrrhus, like the Hyrcanian beast—"
No, that's not it; it begins with Pyrrhus—
"The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose black armor,
black as his purpose, was like the night
when he lay hidden in the fateful horse,
has now this dread and black complexion smeared
with deadlier heraldry. From head to foot
he's now all red, horribly painted over
with the blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,
baked and crusted on by the burning streets,
which lend a cruel and a damned light
to their vile murders. Roasted in wrath and fire,
and thus glazed thick with clotted gore,
with eyes like burning coals, the hellish Pyrrhus
seeks out old grandfather Priam."
Now you go on.

POLONIUS
Before God, my lord, well spoken—with good accent and good judgment.

FIRST PLAYER
"Soon he finds him,
striking too short at the Greeks. His ancient sword,
rebelling against his arm, lies where it falls,
deaf to command. In this unequal match,
Pyrrhus drives at Priam, in his rage strikes wide;
but at the mere whiff and wind of his savage sword
the weak old father falls. Then lifeless Troy,
seeming to feel this blow, with its flaming top
crashes down to its base, and with a hideous roar
takes Pyrrhus's ear prisoner. For look—his sword,
which was coming down on the milk-white head
of venerable Priam, seemed to stick in the air.
So, like a tyrant in a painting, Pyrrhus stood,
and, as if neutral between his will and his task,
did nothing.
But as we often see, before some storm,
a silence in the heavens, the clouds standing still,
the bold winds speechless, and the earth below
as hushed as death—then suddenly the dreadful thunder
splits the sky; so, after Pyrrhus's pause,
roused vengeance sets him back to work,
and never did the Cyclops' hammers fall
on Mars's armor, forged to last forever,
with less mercy than Pyrrhus's bleeding sword
now falls on Priam.
Away, away, you whore Fortune! All you gods,
in full assembly, strip away her power;
break all the spokes and rims from her wheel,
and bowl the round hub down the hill of heaven,
as far down as to hell."

POLONIUS
This is too long.

HAMLET
It shall go to the barber's, along with your beard.—Please, go on. He's only for a jig or a dirty story, or he falls asleep. Go on; come to Hecuba.

FIRST PLAYER
"But who—oh, who—had seen the mobled queen—"

HAMLET
"The mobled queen"?

POLONIUS
That's good! "Mobled queen" is good.

FIRST PLAYER
"running barefoot up and down, threatening the flames
with blinding tears; a rag upon that head
where lately the crown stood; and for a robe,
about her thin and worn-out, much-childbearing waist,
a blanket, snatched up in the panic of fear—
whoever had seen this, with a tongue dipped in venom,
would have proclaimed Fortune's reign a treason.
But if the gods themselves had seen her then,
when she saw Pyrrhus making cruel sport,
hacking her husband's limbs with his sword,
the sudden burst of outcry that she made—
unless mortal things move them not at all—
would have made the burning eyes of heaven weep,
and stirred grief in the gods."

POLONIUS
Look—hasn't he changed color, and got tears in his eyes? Please, no more.

HAMLET
That's well. I'll have you speak the rest of this soon.—Good my lord, will you see the players properly looked after? Do you hear—let them be well used; for they are the summaries and brief chronicles of the age. You had better have a bad epitaph after your death than their ill report while you live.

POLONIUS
My lord, I'll treat them as they deserve.

HAMLET
God's little body, man, much better! Treat every man as he deserves, and who would escape a whipping? Use them after your own honor and dignity. The less they deserve, the more credit is in your generosity. Take them in.

POLONIUS
Come, sirs.

HAMLET
Follow him, friends. We'll hear a play tomorrow.
[_Exeunt Polonius with all the Players but the First._]

HAMLET
Do you hear me, old friend? Can you perform The Murder of Gonzago?

FIRST PLAYER
Ay, my lord.

HAMLET
We'll have it tomorrow night. You could, if needed, learn a speech of some dozen or sixteen lines, which I would write down and insert in it—could you not?

FIRST PLAYER
Ay, my lord.

HAMLET
Very well. Follow that lord—and see you don't mock him.
[_Exit First Player._]

HAMLET
[_To Rosencrantz and Guildenstern._] My good friends, I'll leave you till tonight. You're welcome to Elsinore.

ROSENCRANTZ
Good my lord.
[_Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern._]

HAMLET
Ay, so. God be with you.—Now I am alone.
Oh, what a rogue and peasant slave am I!
Isn't it monstrous that this player here,
in a mere fiction, in a dream of passion,
could force his soul so to his own imagining
that, from its working, all his face went pale,
tears in his eyes, distraction in his look,
a broken voice, and his whole being shaped
to fit his thought? And all for nothing!
For Hecuba!
What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba,
that he should weep for her? What would he do
had he the motive and the cue for passion
that I have? He would drown the stage with tears
and split the general ear with dreadful speech,
drive the guilty mad, and terrify the innocent,
confound the ignorant, and stun, indeed,
the very powers of eyes and ears. Yet I,
a dull and muddy-spirited rascal, mope
like a daydreamer, with nothing to say for my cause,
and can say nothing—no, not for a king
upon whose property and most dear life
a damned defeat was worked. Am I a coward?
Who calls me villain, breaks my skull across,
plucks off my beard and blows it in my face,
tweaks me by the nose, gives me the lie in the throat
as deep as to the lungs? Who does this to me?
Ha! By God's wounds, I'd have to take it; for it must be
that I am pigeon-livered and lack the gall
to make oppression bitter—or before now
I'd have fattened all the kites of the air
with this slave's guts. Bloody, lecherous villain!
Remorseless, treacherous, lustful, unnatural villain!
Oh, vengeance!
Why, what an ass am I! This is most fine—
that I, the son of a dear father murdered,
prompted to my revenge by heaven and hell,
must, like a whore, unpack my heart with words
and fall to cursing like a common slut,
a scullery-maid! Shame on it! Foh!
Get to work, my brain! I have heard
that guilty creatures, sitting at a play,
have, by the very cunning of the scene,
been struck so to the soul that on the spot
they have confessed their crimes;
for murder, though it has no tongue, will speak
