with a most miraculous voice. I'll have these players
play something like the murder of my father
before my uncle. I'll watch his face;
I'll probe him to the quick. If he so much as flinches,
I know my course. The spirit that I've seen
may be the devil; and the devil has the power
to take a pleasing shape; yes, and perhaps,
out of my weakness and my melancholy—
as he is very potent with such moods—
he abuses me to damn me. I'll have grounds
more solid than this. The play's the thing
in which I'll catch the conscience of the King.
[_Exit._]

books.label: Act III
paragraphs: SCENE I. A room in the Castle.
Enter King, Queen, Polonius, Ophelia, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

KING
And can you find no roundabout way
to get from him why he puts on this confusion,
grating so harshly on all his quiet days
with turbulent and dangerous madness?

ROSENCRANTZ
He does admit he feels himself unsettled,
but from what cause he will by no means say.

GUILDENSTERN
Nor do we find him willing to be sounded;
with a crafty madness he keeps his distance
when we would draw him on to some confession
of his true state.

QUEEN
Did he receive you well?

ROSENCRANTZ
Most like a gentleman.

GUILDENSTERN
But with much forcing of himself to it.

ROSENCRANTZ
Sparing with questions, but to ours
most free in his reply.

QUEEN
Did you try to tempt him to any pastime?

ROSENCRANTZ
Madam, it so happened that certain players
we overtook on the way. We told him of these,
and there did seem in him a kind of joy
to hear of it. They are about the court,
and, as I think, already have their orders
to play before him tonight.

POLONIUS
It's most true;
and he begged me to entreat your Majesties
to hear and see the matter.

KING
With all my heart; and it does much content me
to hear him so inclined.
Good gentlemen, give him a further push,
and drive his purpose on toward these delights.

ROSENCRANTZ
We shall, my lord.
[_Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern._]

KING
Sweet Gertrude, leave us too,
for we have secretly sent for Hamlet here,
so that he, as if by accident, may meet
Ophelia face to face.
Her father and myself, lawful spies,
will so place ourselves that, seeing unseen,
we may judge their encounter frankly,
and gather, by how he behaves,
whether it's the affliction of his love or not
that makes him suffer so.

QUEEN
I shall obey you.
And for your part, Ophelia, I do wish
that your good beauty be the happy cause
of Hamlet's wildness; so I hope your virtues
will bring him to his usual self again,
to both your honors.

OPHELIA
Madam, I wish it may.
[_Exit Queen._]

POLONIUS
Ophelia, walk you here.—Gracious, if you please,
we will conceal ourselves.—[_To Ophelia._] Read on this book,
so the show of such devotion may explain
your being alone.—We are often to blame in this:
it's too well proved, that with a face of devotion
and pious action we sugar over
the devil himself.

KING
[_Aside._] Oh, it's too true!
How sharp a lash that speech gives to my conscience!
The harlot's cheek, made beautiful with paint,
is not more ugly next to what helps it
than is my deed beside my most painted word.
O heavy burden!

POLONIUS
I hear him coming. Let's withdraw, my lord.
[_Exeunt King and Polonius._]
Enter Hamlet.

HAMLET
To be, or not to be, that is the question:
Whether it's nobler in the mind to suffer
the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,
or to take arms against a sea of troubles,
and by opposing end them? To die—to sleep,
no more; and by a sleep to say we end
the heartache, and the thousand natural shocks
that flesh is heir to: it's a consummation
devoutly to be wished. To die, to sleep.
To sleep, perchance to dream—ay, there's the rub,
for in that sleep of death what dreams may come,
when we have shuffled off this mortal coil,
must give us pause. There's the consideration
that makes calamity of so long a life.
For who would bear the whips and scorns of time,
the oppressor's wrong, the proud man's contempt,
the pangs of rejected love, the law's delay,
the insolence of office, and the spurns
that patient merit takes from the unworthy,
when he himself might settle his account
with a bare dagger? Who would carry these burdens,
to grunt and sweat under a weary life,
but that the dread of something after death,
the undiscovered country, from whose border
no traveller returns, puzzles the will,
and makes us rather bear those ills we have
than fly to others that we know not of?
Thus conscience does make cowards of us all,
and thus the native hue of resolution
is sicklied over with the pale cast of thought,
and enterprises of great pith and moment,
with this regard their currents turn awry
and lose the name of action. Soft you now,
the fair Ophelia! Nymph, in your prayers
be all my sins remembered.

OPHELIA
Good my lord,
how has your honor been these many days?

HAMLET
I humbly thank you; well, well, well.

OPHELIA
My lord, I have remembrances of yours
that I have long wished to give back to you.
I pray you, now receive them.

HAMLET
No, not I.
I never gave you anything.

OPHELIA
My honored lord, you know right well you did,
and with them words composed of such sweet breath
as made the things more rich; their perfume lost,
take these again; for to the noble mind
rich gifts grow poor when givers prove unkind.
There, my lord.

HAMLET
Ha, ha! Are you honest?

OPHELIA
My lord?

HAMLET
Are you fair?

OPHELIA
What does your lordship mean?

HAMLET
That if you are honest and fair, your honesty should allow no dealings with your beauty.

OPHELIA
Could beauty, my lord, keep better company than with honesty?

HAMLET
Ay, truly; for the power of beauty will sooner turn honesty into a bawd than the force of honesty can make beauty over in its own image. This was once a paradox, but now the times prove it true. I did love you once.

OPHELIA
Indeed, my lord, you made me believe so.

HAMLET
You should not have believed me; for virtue cannot be so grafted onto our old stock but we shall still taste of the wild. I loved you not.

OPHELIA
I was the more deceived.

HAMLET
Get thee to a nunnery. Why would you be a breeder of sinners? I am myself reasonably honest; and yet I could accuse myself of such things that it would have been better my mother had not borne me. I am very proud, revengeful, ambitious, with more offenses at my beck than I have thoughts to put them in, imagination to give them shape, or time to act them in. What should such fellows as I do, crawling between earth and heaven? We are downright knaves, all; believe none of us. Go your ways to a nunnery. Where's your father?

OPHELIA
At home, my lord.

HAMLET
Let the doors be shut on him, so he may play the fool nowhere but in his own house. Farewell.

OPHELIA
Oh, help him, you sweet heavens!

HAMLET
If you do marry, I'll give you this plague for your dowry: be as chaste as ice, as pure as snow, you shall not escape slander. Get thee to a nunnery, go: farewell. Or if you must marry, marry a fool; for wise men know well enough what monsters you make of them. To a nunnery, go; and quickly too. Farewell.

OPHELIA
O heavenly powers, restore him!

HAMLET
I have heard of your paintings too, well enough. God has given you one face, and you make yourselves another. You jig, you sway, and you lisp, and give pet names to God's creatures, and pass off your loose ways as innocence. Go to, I'll have no more of it; it has made me mad. I say, we will have no more marriages. Those that are married already, all but one, shall live; the rest shall stay as they are. To a nunnery, go.
[_Exit._]

OPHELIA
Oh, what a noble mind is here overthrown!
The courtier's, soldier's, scholar's eye, tongue, sword,
the hope and rose of this fair state,
the mirror of fashion and the mold of form,
the one observed by all observers, quite, quite down!
And I, of ladies most dejected and wretched,
who drank the honey of his music vows,
now see that noble and most sovereign reason,
like sweet bells jangled out of tune and harsh,
that unmatched form and feature of full-blown youth
blasted with madness. Oh, woe is me,
to have seen what I have seen, see what I see.
Enter King and Polonius.

KING
Love? His feelings do not tend that way,
nor what he spoke, though it lacked form a little,
was anything like madness. There's something in his soul
over which his melancholy sits brooding,
and I do fear the hatch and the disclosing of it
will be some danger; which to prevent,
I have, in quick decision,
set it down: he shall go with speed to England
to demand the tribute they've neglected.
Perhaps the seas, and different countries,
with their changing sights, shall drive out
this settled something in his heart,
on which his brain keeps beating and so puts him
beside himself. What do you think of it?

POLONIUS
It will do well. But still I do believe
the origin and beginning of his grief
sprang from neglected love.—How now, Ophelia?
You need not tell us what Lord Hamlet said;
we heard it all.—My lord, do as you please,
but if you think it fit, after the play,
let his queen mother, all alone, entreat him
to show his grief; let her be blunt with him,
and I'll be placed, if you please, within hearing
of all their talk. If she find him out no better,
to England send him; or confine him where
your wisdom thinks best.

KING
It shall be so.
Madness in great ones must not go unwatched.
[_Exeunt._]
SCENE II. A hall in the Castle.
Enter Hamlet and certain Players.

HAMLET
Speak the speech, I pray you, as I pronounced it to you, trippingly on the tongue. But if you mouth it, as many of your players do, I would just as soon the town-crier spoke my lines. Nor do not saw the air too much with your hand, like this, but use everything gently; for in the very torrent, tempest, and—as I may say—whirlwind of passion, you must acquire and produce a restraint that gives it smoothness. Oh, it offends me to the soul to hear a robustious, wig-headed fellow tear a passion to tatters, to very rags, to split the ears of the groundlings, who, for the most part, can take in nothing but baffling dumb-shows and noise. I would have such a fellow whipped for overdoing Termagant. It out-Herods Herod. Pray you avoid it.

FIRST PLAYER
I promise you, your honor.

HAMLET
Don't be too tame either; but let your own discretion be your tutor. Suit the action to the word, the word to the action, with this special care, that you don't overstep the modesty of nature; for anything so overdone misses the whole point of playing, whose end, both at the first and now, was and is, to hold, as it were, the mirror up to nature: to show virtue her own feature, scorn her own image, and the very age and body of the time its form and impression. Now, this overdone, or done too feebly, though it make the unskilled laugh, cannot but make the discerning grieve; and the judgment of one of those must, in your reckoning, outweigh a whole theater of the others. Oh, there are players I have seen play—and heard others praise, and highly too—who, not to put it crudely, having neither the speech of Christians, nor the gait of Christian, pagan, nor man, have so strutted and bellowed that I have thought some of Nature's apprentices had made men, and not made them well, they imitated humanity so abominably.

FIRST PLAYER
I hope we have reformed that tolerably well with us, sir.

HAMLET
Oh, reform it altogether. And let those that play your clowns speak no more than is set down for them. For there are some of them that will laugh themselves, just to set a pack of barren spectators laughing too, when in the meantime some necessary point of the play needs to be considered. That's villainous, and shows a most pitiful ambition in the fool that does it. Go make yourselves ready.
[_Exeunt Players._]
Enter Polonius, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

HAMLET
How now, my lord?
Will the King hear this piece of work?

POLONIUS
And the Queen too, and right away.

HAMLET
Tell the players to make haste.
[_Exit Polonius._]

HAMLET
Will you two help to hurry them?

ROSENCRANTZ and GUILDENSTERN
We will, my lord.
[_Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern._]

HAMLET
What ho, Horatio!
Enter Horatio.

HORATIO
Here, sweet lord, at your service.

HAMLET
Horatio, you are as fair a man
as I have ever dealt with in my life.

HORATIO
O my dear lord—

HAMLET
No, do not think I flatter;
for what advancement may I hope from you,
who have no income but your own good spirits
to feed and clothe you? Why should the poor be flattered?
No, let the sugared tongue lick foolish pomp,
and bend the eager hinges of the knee
where profit follows fawning. Do you hear?
Since my dear soul was mistress of her choice,
and could tell one man from another, her election
has sealed you for herself. For you have been
as one who, in suffering everything, suffers nothing,
a man that Fortune's blows and rewards
has taken with equal thanks. And blessed are those
whose blood and judgment are so well mingled
that they are not a pipe for Fortune's finger
to sound what note she pleases. Give me the man
that is not passion's slave, and I will wear him
in my heart's core, ay, in my heart of hearts,
as I do you. But enough of this.
There is a play tonight before the King.
One scene of it comes near the circumstance
which I have told you, of my father's death.
I beg you, when you see that act under way,
with the very closest watching of your soul
observe my uncle. If his hidden guilt
does not unkennel itself at one speech,
it is a damned ghost that we have seen,
and my imaginings are as foul
as Vulcan's forge. Give him your closest note;
for I will rivet my eyes to his face;
and afterward we will both join our judgments
in reckoning how he looked.

HORATIO
Well, my lord.
If he steal anything while this play is playing,
and escape detection, I will pay for the theft.

HAMLET
They are coming to the play. I must act mad.
Get yourself a place.
Danish march. A flourish. Enter King, Queen, Polonius, Ophelia, Rosencrantz, Guildenstern and others.

KING
How fares our cousin Hamlet?

HAMLET
Excellent, in faith; I dine on the chameleon's dish: I eat the air, stuffed with promises. You cannot fatten capons so.

KING
I can make nothing of this answer, Hamlet; these words are not mine.

HAMLET
No, nor mine now. [_To Polonius._] My lord, you acted once at the university, you say?

POLONIUS
That I did, my lord, and was reckoned a good actor.

HAMLET
What did you play?

POLONIUS
I played Julius Caesar. I was killed in the Capitol. Brutus killed me.

HAMLET
It was a brute part of him to kill so capital a calf there. Are the players ready?

ROSENCRANTZ
Ay, my lord; they wait upon your pleasure.

QUEEN
Come here, my dear Hamlet, sit by me.

HAMLET
No, good mother, here's metal more attractive.

POLONIUS
[_To the King._] O ho! Do you mark that?

HAMLET
Lady, shall I lie in your lap?
[_Lying down at Ophelia's feet._]

OPHELIA
No, my lord.

HAMLET
I mean, my head upon your lap?

OPHELIA
Ay, my lord.

HAMLET
Do you think I meant country matters?

OPHELIA
I think nothing, my lord.

HAMLET
That's a fair thought to lie between a maid's legs.

OPHELIA
What is, my lord?

HAMLET
Nothing.

OPHELIA
You are merry, my lord.

HAMLET
Who, I?

OPHELIA
Ay, my lord.

HAMLET
O God, your only jig-maker! What should a man do but be merry? For look how cheerfully my mother looks, and my father dead within these two hours.

OPHELIA
No, it's twice two months, my lord.

HAMLET
So long? Nay, then let the devil wear black, for I'll have a suit of sables. O heavens! Dead two months ago, and not forgotten yet? Then there's hope a great man's memory may outlive his life by half a year. But, by the Lady, he must build churches then, or else he shall get no remembrance, like the hobby-horse, whose epitaph is 'For, O, for O, the hobby-horse is forgot!'
Trumpets sound. The dumb show enters.

_Enter a King and a Queen very lovingly; the Queen embracing him and he her. She kneels, and makes show of protestation unto him. He takes her up, and declines his head upon her neck. Lays him down upon a bank of flowers. She, seeing him asleep, leaves him. Soon a man comes in, takes off his crown, kisses it, pours poison in the King's ears, and exits. The Queen returns, finds the King dead, and makes passionate action. The Poisoner with some three or four Mutes, comes in again, seeming to lament with her. The dead body is carried away. The Poisoner woos the Queen with gifts. She seems reluctant for a while, but in the end accepts his love._
[_Exeunt._]

OPHELIA
What does this mean, my lord?

HAMLET
Marry, this is sneaking mischief; it means trouble.

OPHELIA
Most likely this show sums up the plot of the play.
Enter Prologue.

HAMLET
We shall learn it from this fellow: the players cannot keep a secret; they'll tell all.

OPHELIA
Will they tell us what this show meant?

HAMLET
Ay, or any show that you'll show him. Be not you ashamed to show, and he'll not be ashamed to tell you what it means.

OPHELIA
You are wicked, you are wicked. I'll watch the play.

PROLOGUE
 For us, and for our tragedy,
 here stooping to your clemency,
 we beg your hearing patiently.

HAMLET
Is this a prologue, or the motto on a ring?

OPHELIA
It's brief, my lord.

HAMLET
As a woman's love.
Enter a King and a Queen.

PLAYER KING
Full thirty times has Phoebus' chariot gone round
Neptune's salt tides and Tellus' rounded ground,
and thirty dozen moons with borrowed sheen
about the world twelve times thirty have been,
since love our hearts, and Hymen our hands,
joined mutually in most sacred bands.

PLAYER QUEEN
So many journeys may the sun and moon
make us count over again before love is done.
But, woe is me, you are so sick of late,
so far from cheer and from your former state,
that I distrust you. Yet, though I distrust,
discomfort you, my lord, it never must:
for women's fear and love keep parity,
in nothing at all, or in extremity.
Now what my love is, you have proof to know,
and as my love is sized, my fear is so.
Where love is great, the slightest doubts are fear;
where little fears grow great, great love grows there.

PLAYER KING
In faith, I must leave you, love, and shortly too:
my working powers their functions cease to do;
and you shall live in this fair world behind,
honored, beloved; and perhaps one as kind
for a husband shall you—

PLAYER QUEEN
Oh, say no more!
Such love would be sheer treason in my breast.
In a second husband let me be accursed!
None wed the second but who killed the first.

HAMLET
[_Aside._] Wormwood, wormwood.

PLAYER QUEEN
The motives that move a second marriage
are base concerns of gain, but none of love.
A second time I kill my husband dead,
when a second husband kisses me in bed.

PLAYER KING
I do believe you think what now you speak;
but what we resolve, we often break.
Purpose is but the slave to memory,
of violent birth, but poor durability:
which now, like fruit unripe, sticks on the tree,
but falls unshaken when it ripe shall be.
It's most necessary that we forget
to pay ourselves what to ourselves is debt.
What to ourselves in passion we propose,
the passion ending, does the purpose lose.
The violence of either grief or joy
does its own intent itself destroy.
Where joy most revels, grief does most lament;
grief turns to joy, joy grieves, on slight event.
This world is not forever; nor is it strange
that even our loves should with our fortunes change,
for it's a question still left us to prove,
whether love leads fortune, or fortune love.
The great man down, you see his favorite flies;
the poor man, raised, makes friends of enemies.
And so far love does upon fortune tend;
for who needs nothing shall never lack a friend,
and who in want a hollow friend does try
at once converts him to an enemy.
But, to end in order where I begun:
our wills and fates so contrary run
that all our plans are constantly overthrown;
our thoughts are ours, their ends are not our own.
So think you will no second husband wed;
but let that thought die when your first lord is dead.

PLAYER QUEEN
May earth give me no food, nor heaven light,
may sport and rest be locked from me day and night,
may my trust and hope turn to despair,
an anchorite's bare cell be all my fare,
may each opposite that drains the face of joy
meet what I would have prosper, and destroy it!
Both here and beyond pursue me lasting strife,
if, once a widow, ever I be wife.

HAMLET
[_To Ophelia._] If she should break it now.

PLAYER KING
It's deeply sworn. Sweet, leave me here awhile;
my spirits grow dull, and I would gladly cheat
the tedious day with sleep.
[_Sleeps._]

PLAYER QUEEN
Sleep rock your brain,
and never come mischance between us two.
[_Exit._]

HAMLET
Madam, how do you like this play?

QUEEN
The lady protests too much, methinks.

HAMLET
Oh, but she'll keep her word.

KING
Have you heard the plot? Is there no offense in it?

HAMLET
No, no, they only jest, poison in jest; no offense in the world.

KING
What do you call the play?

HAMLET
_The Mousetrap._ Marry, how so? In a manner of speaking. This play is the image of a murder done in Vienna. Gonzago is the duke's name, his wife Baptista. You shall see soon enough; it's a knavish piece of work, but what of that? Your Majesty, and we that have clear consciences, it doesn't touch us. Let the galled horse wince; our backs are unbruised.
Enter Lucianus.

HAMLET
This is one Lucianus, nephew to the King.

OPHELIA
You are as good as a chorus, my lord.

HAMLET
I could interpret between you and your love, if I could watch the puppets dallying.

OPHELIA
You are sharp, my lord, you are sharp.

HAMLET
It would cost you a groan to take off my edge.

OPHELIA
Still better, and worse.

HAMLET
So you mis-take your husbands.—Begin, murderer. Pox, leave your damnable faces, and begin. Come: the croaking raven bellows for revenge.

LUCIANUS
Thoughts black, hands ready, drugs fit, and the time agreeing;
the moment my ally, and no creature seeing;
you rank mixture, of midnight weeds collected,
with Hecate's curse thrice blasted, thrice infected,
your natural magic and dire property
on wholesome life now seize immediately.
[_Pours the poison into the sleeper's ears._]

HAMLET
He poisons him in the garden for his estate. His name's Gonzago. The story is on record, and written in very choice Italian. You shall see soon how the murderer wins the love of Gonzago's wife.

OPHELIA
The King rises.

HAMLET
What, frightened by a blank shot?

QUEEN
How fares my lord?

POLONIUS
Stop the play.

KING
Give me some light. Away.

All
Lights, lights, lights.
[_Exeunt all but Hamlet and Horatio._]

HORATIO
Half a share.

HAMLET
A whole one, I.
 For you do know, O Damon dear,
 this realm was stripped clean
 of Jove himself, and now reigns here
 a very, very—peacock.

HORATIO
You might have rhymed.

HAMLET
O good Horatio, I'll take the ghost's word for a thousand pounds. Did you notice?

HORATIO
Very well, my lord.

HAMLET
When the talk turned to the poisoning?

HORATIO
I watched him very closely.

HAMLET
Ah, ha! Come, some music. Come, the recorders.
 For if the King doesn't like the comedy,
 why then, it seems he likes it not, by God.
Come, some music.
Enter Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

GUILDENSTERN
Good my lord, grant me a word with you.

HAMLET
Sir, a whole history.

GUILDENSTERN
The King, sir—

HAMLET
Ay, sir, what of him?

GUILDENSTERN
Is in his chambers, marvelously out of sorts.

HAMLET
With drink, sir?

GUILDENSTERN
No, my lord; rather with anger.

HAMLET
Your wisdom would show itself the richer to report this to the doctor; for me to give him his cure would perhaps plunge him into far more anger.

GUILDENSTERN
Good my lord, put your talk into some order, and don't start off so wildly from my business.

HAMLET
I am tame, sir; speak.

GUILDENSTERN
The Queen your mother, in great affliction of spirit, has sent me to you.

HAMLET
You are welcome.

GUILDENSTERN
Nay, good my lord, this courtesy is not of the honest kind. If it shall please you to give me a sensible answer, I will do your mother's bidding; if not, your pardon and my leaving shall be the end of my business.

HAMLET
Sir, I cannot.

GUILDENSTERN
Cannot what, my lord?

HAMLET
Give you a sensible answer. My wit's diseased. But, sir, such answer as I can make, you shall command; or rather, as you say, my mother shall. So no more, but to the matter. My mother, you say—

ROSENCRANTZ
Then thus she says: your behavior has struck her into amazement and bewilderment.

HAMLET
O wonderful son, who can so astonish a mother! But is there nothing following at the heels of this mother's amazement?

ROSENCRANTZ
She desires to speak with you in her room before you go to bed.

HAMLET
We shall obey, were she ten times our mother. Have you any further business with us?

ROSENCRANTZ
My lord, you once did love me.

HAMLET
And so I do still, by these fingers of mine that pick and steal.

ROSENCRANTZ
Good my lord, what is the cause of your distemper? You surely bar the door upon your own freedom if you deny your griefs to your friend.

HAMLET
Sir, I lack advancement.

ROSENCRANTZ
How can that be, when you have the voice of the King himself for your succession in Denmark?

HAMLET
Ay, sir, but 'while the grass grows'—the proverb is a little stale.
Re-enter the Players with recorders.

HAMLET
Oh, the recorders. Let me see one.—To have a word with you in private: why do you go about to get to windward of me, as if you would drive me into a trap?

GUILDENSTERN
O my lord, if my duty is too bold, my love is too unmannerly.

HAMLET
I don't quite understand that. Will you play upon this pipe?

GUILDENSTERN
My lord, I cannot.

HAMLET
I pray you.

GUILDENSTERN
Believe me, I cannot.

HAMLET
I do beseech you.

GUILDENSTERN
I know no touch of it, my lord.

HAMLET
It's as easy as lying: govern these vents with your finger and thumb, give it breath with your mouth, and it will speak most eloquent music. Look you, these are the stops.

GUILDENSTERN
But these I cannot command to make any harmony. I haven't the skill.

HAMLET
Why, look you now, what an unworthy thing you make of me! You would play upon me; you would seem to know my stops; you would pluck out the heart of my mystery; you would sound me from my lowest note to the top of my range; and there is much music, excellent voice, in this little instrument, yet you cannot make it speak. By God's blood, do you think I am easier to be played on than a pipe? Call me what instrument you will: though you can fret me, you cannot play upon me.
Enter Polonius.

HAMLET
God bless you, sir.

POLONIUS
My lord, the Queen would speak with you, and right away.

HAMLET
Do you see that cloud over there, almost in the shape of a camel?

POLONIUS
By the mass, it's like a camel indeed.

HAMLET
I think it's like a weasel.

POLONIUS
It's backed like a weasel.

HAMLET
Or like a whale.

POLONIUS
Very like a whale.

HAMLET
Then I'll come to my mother shortly.—They make me play the fool to the top of my bent.—I will come shortly.

POLONIUS
I'll say so.
[_Exit._]

HAMLET
'Shortly' is easily said. Leave me, friends.
[_Exeunt all but Hamlet._]

HAMLET
It's now the very witching time of night,
when churchyards yawn, and hell itself breathes out
contagion to this world. Now could I drink hot blood,
and do such bitter business as the day
would tremble to look on. Soft, now, to my mother.
O heart, do not lose your nature; never let
the soul of Nero enter this firm breast.
Let me be cruel, not unnatural.
I will speak daggers to her, but use none;
my tongue and soul in this be hypocrites.
However my words may shame her,
to seal them with deeds, my soul, never consent.
[_Exit._]
SCENE III. A room in the Castle.
Enter King, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

KING
I like him not, nor is it safe for us
to let his madness range. So prepare yourselves;
I'll dispatch your commission at once,
and he shall go along with you to England.
The interests of our state cannot endure
a danger so near us as grows by the hour
out of his lunacies.

GUILDENSTERN
We will get ready.
It's a most holy and religious fear,
to keep so many, many bodies safe
that live and feed upon your Majesty.

ROSENCRANTZ
The single, private life is bound
with all the strength and armor of the mind
to keep itself from harm; but how much more
that spirit on whose welfare rest and depend
the lives of many. The death of a king
dies not alone, but, like a whirlpool, draws
what's near it down with it. It is a massive wheel,
fixed on the summit of the highest mount,
to whose huge spokes ten thousand lesser things
are fastened and joined; and when it falls,
each small attachment, every petty consequence,
follows in the violent ruin. The King never sighed alone,
but always with a general groan.

ROSENCRANTZ and GUILDENSTERN
We will make haste.
[_Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern._]
Enter Polonius.

POLONIUS
My lord, he's going to his mother's room.
Behind the tapestry I'll hide myself
to hear how it goes. I'll warrant she'll take him to task;
and, as you said—and wisely was it said—
it's fitting that some ear besides a mother's,
since nature makes them partial, should overhear
the talk from a place of vantage. Fare you well, my liege;
I'll call on you before you go to bed,
and tell you what I learn.

KING
Thanks, dear my lord.
[_Exit Polonius._]

KING
Oh, my offense is rank, it smells to heaven;
it bears the primal, eldest curse upon it—
a brother's murder! Pray I cannot,
though my desire be as sharp as my will:
my stronger guilt defeats my strong intent,
and, like a man bound to two tasks at once,
I stand and pause where I should first begin,
and do neither. What if this cursed hand
were thicker than itself with brother's blood—
is there not rain enough in the sweet heavens
to wash it white as snow? What is mercy for
but to face the offense head-on?
And what's in prayer but this twofold power,
to stop us before we fall,
or pardon us once we're down? Then I'll look up.
My fault is past. But, oh, what form of prayer
can serve my turn? 'Forgive me my foul murder'?
That cannot be; since I am still possessed
of those very things for which I did the murder—
my crown, my own ambition, and my queen.
May one be pardoned and keep the offense?
In the corrupted currents of this world
the gilded hand of crime may shove justice aside,
and often it's seen the wicked prize itself
buys out the law. But it's not so above:
there is no dodging there; the deed lies exposed
in its true nature, and we ourselves are forced,
even to the teeth and forehead of our faults,
to give evidence. What then? What's left?
Try what repentance can. What can it not?
Yet what can it, when one cannot repent?
O wretched state! O breast as black as death!
O limed soul, that, struggling to be free,
becomes more trapped! Help, angels! Make the attempt:
bow, stubborn knees; and heart with strings of steel,
be soft as the sinews of a new-born babe.
All may be well.
[_Retires and kneels._]
Enter Hamlet.

HAMLET
Now might I do it neatly, now he is praying.
And now I'll do it. And so he goes to heaven;
and so am I revenged. That would be worth a thought:
a villain kills my father, and for that
I, his sole son, send this same villain
to heaven. Oh, this is wages and reward, not revenge.
He caught my father gross, full-fed,
with all his sins in full bloom, fresh as May;
and how his account stands, who knows but heaven?
But by our understanding and our reckoning,
it goes hard with him. And am I then revenged,
to take him in the cleansing of his soul,
when he is fit and ready for his passage? No.
Up, sword, and wait to strike a more horrid blow:
when he is drunk asleep, or in his rage,
or in the incestuous pleasure of his bed,
at gambling, swearing, or about some act
that has no taste of salvation in it—
then trip him, so his heels may kick at heaven,
and his soul may be as damned and black
as hell, where it is going. My mother waits.
This medicine only prolongs your sickly days.
[_Exit._]
The King rises and advances.

KING
My words fly up, my thoughts remain below.
Words without thoughts never to heaven go.
[_Exit._]
SCENE IV. Another room in the Castle.
Enter Queen and Polonius.

POLONIUS
He will come straight. Be sure you press him hard;
tell him his pranks have been too gross to bear,
and that your Grace has screened and stood between
much heat and him. I'll keep silent right here.
Pray you be blunt with him.

HAMLET
[_Within._] Mother, mother, mother.

QUEEN
I'll warrant you; have no fear of me.
Withdraw, I hear him coming.
[_Polonius goes behind the arras._]
Enter Hamlet.

HAMLET
Now, mother, what's the matter?

QUEEN
Hamlet, you have your father much offended.

HAMLET
Mother, you have my father much offended.

QUEEN
Come, come, you answer with an idle tongue.

HAMLET
Go, go, you question with a wicked tongue.

QUEEN
Why, how now, Hamlet?

HAMLET
What's the matter now?

QUEEN
Have you forgotten me?

HAMLET
No, by the holy cross, not so.
You are the Queen, your husband's brother's wife;
and—would it were not so—you are my mother.

QUEEN
Nay, then I'll set those on you that can speak.

HAMLET
Come, come, and sit you down; you shall not budge.
You go not till I set you up a mirror
where you may see the inmost part of you.

QUEEN
What will you do? You will not murder me?
Help, help, ho!

POLONIUS
[_Behind._] What, ho! Help, help, help!

HAMLET
How now? A rat? [_Draws._]
Dead, for a ducat, dead!
[_Makes a pass through the arras._]

POLONIUS
[_Behind._] Oh, I am slain!
[_Falls and dies._]

QUEEN
O me, what have you done?

HAMLET
Nay, I don't know. Is it the King?
[_Draws forth Polonius._]

QUEEN
Oh, what a rash and bloody deed is this!

HAMLET
A bloody deed. Almost as bad, good mother,
as kill a king, and marry with his brother.

QUEEN
As kill a king?

HAMLET
Ay, lady, that was my word.—
[_To Polonius._] You wretched, rash, intruding fool, farewell!
I took you for your better. Take your fortune;
you find that being too busy is some danger.—
Leave wringing of your hands. Peace, sit you down,
and let me wring your heart; for so I shall,
if it be made of penetrable stuff,
if damned habit has not brazed it over
so that it's proof and bulwark against all feeling.

QUEEN
What have I done, that you dare wag your tongue
in sound so rude against me?

HAMLET
Such an act
that blurs the grace and blush of modesty,
calls virtue a hypocrite, takes the rose
from the fair forehead of an innocent love
and sets a blister there; makes marriage vows
as false as gamblers' oaths. Oh, such a deed
as plucks the very soul out of the body
of the marriage bond, and makes sweet religion
a mere rhapsody of words. Heaven's face glows red;
yes, this solid world, this mass of matter,
with a face of grief, as though Judgment Day were near,
is sick at heart at the act.

QUEEN
Ah me, what act,
that roars so loud, and thunders even in the prologue?

HAMLET
Look here upon this picture, and on this,
the painted likeness of two brothers.
See what a grace was seated on this brow:
Hyperion's curls, the very forehead of Jove,
an eye like Mars, to threaten and command,
a bearing like the herald Mercury
newly alighted on a heaven-kissing hill—
a combination and a form indeed
where every god did seem to set his seal,
to give the world assurance of a man.
This was your husband. Look you now what follows.
Here is your husband, like a mildewed ear of grain,
blighting his wholesome brother. Have you eyes?
Could you stop feeding on this fair mountain,
and gorge yourself on this moor? Ha! Have you eyes?
You cannot call it love; for at your age
the heyday in the blood is tame, it's humble,
and waits upon the judgment. And what judgment
would step from this to this? You have senses, surely,
or you could not move; but surely that sense
is paralyzed, for madness would not so err,
nor were the senses ever so enslaved by frenzy
but they kept back some measure of choice
to tell so plain a difference. What devil was it
that tricked you so at blind man's bluff?
Eyes without feeling, feeling without sight,
ears without hands or eyes, smell without all,
or but a sickly part of one true sense,
could not so blunder. O shame! Where is your blush?
Rebellious hell,
if you can mutiny in a matron's bones,
then to flaming youth let virtue be as wax
and melt in its own fire. Cry no shame
when the driving heat gives the command,
since frost itself burns just as actively,
and reason acts as pimp to desire.

QUEEN
O Hamlet, speak no more.
You turn my eyes into my very soul,
and there I see such black and ingrained spots
as will not lose their stain.

HAMLET
Nay, but to live
in the rank sweat of a greasy bed,
stewed in corruption, honeying and making love
over the filthy sty—

QUEEN
Oh, speak to me no more!
These words like daggers enter in my ears.
No more, sweet Hamlet.

HAMLET
A murderer and a villain;
a slave that is not one-twentieth the tenth part
of your former lord; a clown of a king;
a cutpurse of the empire and the rule,
who from a shelf the precious crown stole
and put it in his pocket—

QUEEN
No more!

HAMLET
A king of shreds and patches!—
Enter Ghost.

HAMLET
Save me, and hover over me with your wings,
you heavenly guards! What would your gracious figure?

QUEEN
Alas, he's mad.

HAMLET
Do you not come to chide your tardy son,
that, letting time and passion slip, lets go
the urgent acting of your dread command?
Oh, say!

GHOST
Do not forget. This visitation
is but to whet your almost blunted purpose.
But look, amazement sits upon your mother.
Oh, step between her and her struggling soul.
Imagination works strongest in the weakest bodies.
Speak to her, Hamlet.

HAMLET
How is it with you, lady?

QUEEN
Alas, how is it with you,
that you fix your eye on empty air,
and hold conversation with the bodiless wind?
Out at your eyes your spirits wildly peer,
and, like sleeping soldiers roused by the alarm,
your lying hair, as if it had life of its own,
starts up and stands on end. O gentle son,
upon the heat and flame of your distemper
sprinkle cool patience. What is it you look at?

HAMLET
On him, on him! Look how pale he glares.
His form and his cause joined, preaching to stones,
would make them feel.—Do not look upon me,
lest with this piteous sight you turn me
from my stern purpose. Then what I have to do
will lose its true color: tears, perhaps, for blood.

QUEEN
To whom do you say this?

HAMLET
Do you see nothing there?

QUEEN
Nothing at all; yet all that's there, I see.

HAMLET
Nor did you hear anything?

QUEEN
No, nothing but ourselves.

HAMLET
Why, look you there! Look how it steals away!
My father, in the very clothes he wore alive!
Look, where he goes, even now, out at the door!
[_Exit Ghost._]

QUEEN
This is the very invention of your brain.
This bodiless creation madness
is very skilled at making.

HAMLET
Madness!
My pulse, like yours, keeps temperate time,
and makes as healthful music. It is not madness
that I have spoken. Put me to the test,
and I will say the whole matter over again,
which madness would skip from. Mother, for the love of grace,
lay not that flattering unction on your soul,
that it's my madness, not your trespass, speaking.
It will only skin and film the ulcerous place,
while rank corruption, mining all within,
infects unseen. Confess yourself to heaven;
repent what's past; avoid what is to come;
and do not spread the compost on the weeds
to make them ranker. Forgive me this, my virtue;
for in the fatness of these bloated times
virtue itself must beg pardon of vice,
yes, bow and court it for leave to do it good.

QUEEN
O Hamlet, you have cleft my heart in two.

HAMLET
Oh, throw away the worser part of it,
and live the purer with the other half.
Good night. But do not go to my uncle's bed.
Assume a virtue, if you have it not.
That monster, custom, who devours all sense
of evil habits, is yet an angel in this:
that to the practice of fair and good actions
he likewise gives a coat, or uniform,
that is easily put on. Refrain tonight,
and that shall lend a kind of easiness
to the next abstinence; the next still easier;
for habit can almost change the very stamp of nature,
and either curb the devil, or throw him out
with wondrous force. Once more, good night;
and when you are willing to be blessed,
I'll beg a blessing of you.—For this same lord,
[_Pointing to Polonius._]
I do repent; but heaven has so pleased,
to punish me with this, and this with me,
that I must be their scourge and minister.
I will dispose of him, and will answer well
the death I gave him. So, again, good night.
I must be cruel, only to be kind.
Thus bad begins, and worse remains behind.
One word more, good lady.

QUEEN
What shall I do?

HAMLET
Not this, by any means, that I tell you to do:
let the bloated King tempt you again to bed;
pinch your cheek wantonly; call you his mouse;
and let him, for a pair of filthy kisses,
or paddling in your neck with his damned fingers,
make you unravel the whole matter out—
that I am not essentially in madness,
but mad by craft. It would be good to let him know;
for who that's but a queen, fair, sober, wise,
would from a toad, from a bat, a tomcat,
hide such weighty matters? Who would do so?
No, in spite of sense and secrecy,
unlatch the basket on the housetop,
let the birds fly, and like the famous ape,
to test the outcome, creep into the basket
and break your own neck in the fall.

QUEEN
Be assured, if words are made of breath,
and breath of life, I have no life to breathe
what you have said to me.

HAMLET
I must go to England; you know that?

QUEEN
Alack,
I had forgotten. It's so decided.

HAMLET
There are letters sealed; and my two schoolfellows—
whom I will trust as I would adders fanged—
they carry the orders; they must clear my way
and usher me toward some trap. Let it work;
for it's the sport to have the engineer
hoist with his own petard; and it shall go hard
but I will dig one yard below their mines
and blow them at the moon. Oh, it's most sweet
when in one line two plots directly meet.
This man shall set me on my way.
I'll lug the guts into the neighboring room.
Mother, good night. Indeed, this counsellor
is now most still, most secret, and most grave,
who was in life a foolish, prating knave.
Come, sir, to make an end with you.
Good night, mother.
[_Exit Hamlet dragging out Polonius._]

books.label: Act IV
paragraphs: SCENE I. A room in the Castle.
Enter King, Queen, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

KING
There's meaning in these sighs. These heavy heaves
you must explain; it's right that we should understand them.
Where is your son?

QUEEN
Leave us alone here for a little while.
[_To Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, who go out._]
Ah, my good lord, what have I seen tonight!

KING
What, Gertrude? How is Hamlet?

QUEEN
Mad as the sea and wind, when both of them strive
over which is the stronger. In his lawless fit,
hearing something stir behind the tapestry,
he whips out his rapier, cries 'A rat, a rat!'
and in that frenzied notion kills
the unseen good old man.

KING
Oh, terrible deed!
It would have been so with us, had we been there.
His freedom is full of threats to us all—
to you yourself, to us, to everyone.
Alas, how shall this bloody deed be answered for?
It will be laid on us, whose foresight
should have kept this mad young man on a short rein,
restrained, and out of the way. But our love was so great
we would not face what was the wisest course,
but, like the owner of a foul disease
who keeps it from being known, let it feed
even on the very pith of life. Where has he gone?

QUEEN
To drag away the body he has killed—
over which his very madness, like a vein of gold
running through a seam of baser metals,
shows itself pure. He weeps for what he's done.

KING
O Gertrude, come away!
The sun shall no sooner touch the mountains
than we'll ship him out of here; and this vile deed
we must, with all our majesty and skill,
both sanction and excuse.—Ho, Guildenstern!
Re-enter Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

Friends, both of you, go get some further help:
Hamlet in his madness has slain Polonius,
and from his mother's chamber he has dragged him.
Go seek him out, speak gently, and bring the body
into the chapel. Please, be quick about this.
[_Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern._]

Come, Gertrude, we'll call up our wisest friends,
and let them know both what we mean to do
and what's been done before its time—so that slander,
whose whisper carries across the world's full breadth,
as straight as the cannon to its mark,
carrying its poisoned shot, may miss our name
and strike the wound-proof air instead. Oh, come away!
My soul is full of discord and dismay.
[_Exeunt._]
SCENE II. Another room in the Castle.
Enter Hamlet.

HAMLET
Safely stowed.

ROSENCRANTZ and GUILDENSTERN
[_Within._] Hamlet! Lord Hamlet!

HAMLET
What noise? Who's calling for Hamlet? Oh, here they come.
Enter Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.

ROSENCRANTZ
What have you done, my lord, with the dead body?

HAMLET
Mixed it back into the dust it's kin to.

ROSENCRANTZ
Tell us where it is, so that we can take it from there
and carry it to the chapel.

HAMLET
Don't count on it.

ROSENCRANTZ
Count on what?

HAMLET
That I can keep your secrets and not my own. Besides, when a sponge puts the question to me—what answer should be given by the son of a king?

ROSENCRANTZ
Do you take me for a sponge, my lord?

HAMLET
Ay, sir—one that soaks up the King's favor, his rewards, his powers. But officers like that serve the King best in the end: he keeps them, like an ape keeps food, in the corner of his jaw—first into the mouth, last to be swallowed. When he needs what you've gathered up, it's only a matter of squeezing you, and then, sponge, you'll be dry again.

ROSENCRANTZ
I don't understand you, my lord.

HAMLET
I'm glad of it. A sly speech sleeps unheard in a fool's ear.

ROSENCRANTZ
My lord, you must tell us where the body is and come with us to the King.

HAMLET
The body is with the King, but the King is not with the body. The King is a thing—

GUILDENSTERN
A thing, my lord!

HAMLET
Of nothing. Bring me to him. Hide fox, and all after.
[_Exeunt._]
SCENE III. Another room in the Castle.
Enter King, attended.

KING
I've sent men to seek him out and to find the body.
How dangerous it is that this man goes free!
Yet we must not bring the full force of law down on him:
he's loved by the bewildered crowd,
who choose not by their judgment but their eyes;
and where that's so, it's the offender's punishment they weigh,
and never the offense. To keep it all smooth and even,
this sudden sending-away of his must look like
a considered decision. Desperate diseases
are relieved by desperate remedies—
or not at all.
Enter Rosencrantz.
Well? What's happened?

ROSENCRANTZ
Where the dead body's been stowed, my lord,
we cannot get out of him.

KING
But where is he?

ROSENCRANTZ
Outside, my lord, under guard, awaiting your pleasure.

KING
Bring him before us.

ROSENCRANTZ
Ho, Guildenstern! Bring in my lord.
Enter Hamlet and Guildenstern.

KING
Now, Hamlet, where's Polonius?

HAMLET
At supper.

KING
At supper? Where?

HAMLET
Not where he eats, but where he's being eaten. A certain assembly of statesmanlike worms is right now at work on him. Your worm is your only true emperor when it comes to diet. We fatten all other creatures to fatten ourselves, and we fatten ourselves for maggots. Your fat king and your lean beggar are just two courses—two dishes, but to one table. That's the end of it.

KING
Alas, alas!

HAMLET
A man may fish with a worm that has eaten of a king, and eat of the fish that has fed on that worm.

KING
What do you mean by this?

HAMLET
Nothing—only to show you how a king may go on a royal progress through the guts of a beggar.

KING
Where is Polonius?

HAMLET
In heaven. Send someone there to see. If your messenger doesn't find him there, look for him in the other place yourself. But really, if you don't find him within the month, you'll smell him as you go up the stairs into the lobby.

KING
[_To some Attendants._] Go seek him there.

HAMLET
He'll wait till you come.
[_Exeunt Attendants._]

KING
Hamlet, this deed—for your own special safety,
which we hold dear, even as we deeply grieve
for what you've done—must send you away from here
with fiery speed. So get yourself ready;
the ship is waiting, and the wind stands fair,
your companions are ready, and everything is set
for England.

HAMLET
For England?

KING
Ay, Hamlet.

HAMLET
Good.

KING
So it is, if you knew our purposes.

HAMLET
I see a cherub that sees them. But—come; off to England! Farewell, dear mother.

KING
Your loving father, Hamlet.

HAMLET
My mother. Father and mother are man and wife; man and wife are one flesh; and so—my mother. Come, off to England.
[_Exit._]

KING
Follow him close. Lure him aboard with speed;
don't delay it; I'll have him gone tonight.
Away—everything else that hangs on this affair
is sealed and done. Please, make haste.
[_Exeunt Rosencrantz and Guildenstern._]

And England—if you value my friendship at all
(and my great power may well make you feel it,
since your scar still looks raw and red
after the Danish sword, and your free homage
pays its respects to us)—you may not coldly slight
our sovereign command, which fully demands,
by letters pressing to that effect,
the immediate death of Hamlet. Do it, England;
for he rages in my blood like a fever,
and you must cure me. Until I know it's done,
whatever my fortunes, my joy has not begun.
[_Exit._]
SCENE IV. A plain in Denmark.
Enter Fortinbras and Forces marching.

FORTINBRAS
Go, Captain, and greet the Danish king for me.
Tell him that, by his leave, Fortinbras
requests the promised right of passage
across his kingdom. You know the meeting place.
If his Majesty would have anything of us,
we'll pay our respects in person before him;
and let him know as much.

CAPTAIN
I'll do it, my lord.

FORTINBRAS
Move on, gently.
[_Exeunt all but the Captain._]
Enter Hamlet, Rosencrantz, Guildenstern &c.

HAMLET
Good sir, whose forces are these?

CAPTAIN
They're Norway's, sir.

HAMLET
What's their purpose, sir, may I ask?

CAPTAIN
Against some part of Poland.

HAMLET
Who commands them, sir?

CAPTAIN
The nephew of old Norway, Fortinbras.

HAMLET
Is it against the heart of Poland, sir,
or only some border region?

CAPTAIN
To speak truly, and with nothing added,
we go to win a little patch of ground
that holds no profit in it but the name.
I wouldn't rent it for five ducats—five;
nor would it bring to Norway or the Pole
a better price, if it were sold outright.

HAMLET
Why, then the Pole will never bother to defend it.

CAPTAIN
Yes—it's already garrisoned.

HAMLET
Two thousand souls and twenty thousand ducats
won't settle this quarrel over a straw!
This is the abscess of too much wealth and peace,
that breaks inward, and shows no outward cause
for why the man dies. I humbly thank you, sir.

CAPTAIN
God be with you, sir.
[_Exit._]

ROSENCRANTZ
Will it please you to go, my lord?

HAMLET
I'll be right with you. Go on a little ahead.
[_Exeunt all but Hamlet._]

How all occasions do inform against me,
and spur my dull revenge. What is a man,
if the best use and profit of his time
is only to sleep and feed? A beast, no more.
Surely he that made us with such broad reason,
able to look before and after, did not give us
that capability and godlike reason
to let it mold in us, unused. Now whether it's
beastlike forgetfulness, or some cowardly scruple
of thinking too precisely on the outcome—
a thought which, split in four, has one part wisdom
and ever three parts coward—I do not know
why I still live to say 'this thing's to do,'
since I have cause, and will, and strength, and means
to do it. Examples as plain as the earth urge me on:
witness this army of such size and cost,
led by a delicate and tender prince,
whose spirit, swelled with godlike ambition,
makes faces at the unknown outcome,
exposing all that's mortal and unsure
to everything that fortune, death, and danger dare,
and all for an eggshell. To be truly great
is not to stir without great cause,
but greatly to find quarrel in a straw
when honor's at the stake. Where do I stand, then—
I, who have a father killed, a mother stained,
spurs to my reason and my blood,
and let it all sleep, while to my shame I see
the imminent death of twenty thousand men
who, for a fantasy and trick of fame,
go to their graves like beds, fight for a plot
on which the numbers cannot even contest the cause,
which is not tomb enough, nor ground enough,
to hide the slain? Oh, from this time forth,
let my thoughts be bloody, or be nothing worth!
[_Exit._]
SCENE V. Elsinore. A room in the Castle.
Enter Queen, Horatio and a Gentleman.

QUEEN
I will not speak with her.

GENTLEMAN
She insists, and indeed she's out of her mind.
Her state can't help but stir your pity.

QUEEN
What does she want?

GENTLEMAN
She speaks much of her father; says she hears
there are tricks in the world, and clears her throat, and beats her breast,
takes spiteful offense at trifles, says things in riddles
that make only half-sense. Her speech is nothing,
yet the disordered use of it does move
her hearers to draw their own conclusions; they guess at it,
and patch her words together to fit their own thoughts—
which, by her winks and nods and gestures,
really would make one think there might be meaning there,
nothing certain, yet much, and unhappily.
It would be good if she were spoken with, for she may scatter
dangerous suspicions in ill-meaning minds.

QUEEN
Let her come in.
[_Exit Gentleman._]

To my sick soul (as is the very nature of sin),
each trifle seems the prologue to some great disaster.
Guilt is so full of clumsy suspicion
that it spills itself in the fear of being spilled.
Enter Ophelia.

OPHELIA
Where is the beautiful Majesty of Denmark?

QUEEN
How now, Ophelia?

OPHELIA
[_Sings._]
How should I your true love know
from any other one?
By his cockle hat and staff
and his sandal shoes.

QUEEN
Alas, sweet lady, what does this song mean?

OPHELIA
What's that? No—please, listen.
[_Sings._]
He is dead and gone, lady,
he is dead and gone;
at his head a grass-green turf,
at his heels a stone.

QUEEN
No, but Ophelia—

OPHELIA
Please, listen.
[_Sings._]
White his shroud as the mountain snow—
Enter King.

QUEEN
Alas, look here, my lord!

OPHELIA
[_Sings._]
strewn all over with sweet flowers;
which did not go to the grave bewept
with true-love's showers.

KING
How are you, pretty lady?

OPHELIA
Well, God reward you! They say the owl was a baker's daughter. Lord, we know what we are, but know not what we may be. God be at your table!

KING
Her mind is fixed on her father.

OPHELIA
Please, let's have no talk of this; but when they ask you what it means, say this:
[_Sings._]
Tomorrow is Saint Valentine's day,
all in the morning betime,
and I a maid at your window,
to be your Valentine.

Then up he rose and put on his clothes,
and opened the chamber door,
let in the maid, that out a maid
never departed more.

KING
Pretty Ophelia!

OPHELIA
Indeed, without an oath, I'll make an end of it.
[_Sings._]
By Jesus and by Saint Charity,
alas, and for shame!
Young men will do it if they come to it;
by Cock, they are to blame.

She said, before you tumbled me,
you promised me to wed.
So would I have done, by yonder sun,
if you'd not come to my bed.

KING
How long has she been like this?

OPHELIA
I hope all will be well. We must be patient. But I can't help weeping, to think they would lay him in the cold ground. My brother shall know of it. And so I thank you for your good advice. Come, my coach! Good night, ladies; good night, sweet ladies; good night, good night.
[_Exit._]

KING
Follow her close; keep good watch on her, I beg you.
[_Exit Horatio._]

Oh, this is the poison of deep grief; it springs
entirely from her father's death. O Gertrude, Gertrude,
when sorrows come, they come not single spies,
but in battalions. First, her father slain;
next, your son gone—and he the most violent cause
of his own just removal; the people stirred up,
muddied, and unwholesome in their thoughts and whispers
about good Polonius's death. And we have acted rashly
in burying him in such secret haste. Poor Ophelia,
divided from herself and her sound judgment,
without which we are mere pictures, or mere beasts.
Last, and weighing as much as all of these,
her brother has come secretly back from France,
feeds on his amazement, keeps himself in shadow,
and has no shortage of gossips to infect his ear
with poisonous talk about his father's death—
in which gossip, starved for facts,
won't scruple to accuse our person,
whispering ear to ear. O my dear Gertrude, all this,
like grapeshot from a cannon, in many places
deals me more deaths than I need.
[_A noise within._]

QUEEN
Alas, what noise is this?

KING
Where are my Swiss guards? Let them guard the door.
Enter a Gentleman.
What's the matter?

GENTLEMAN
Save yourself, my lord.
The ocean, overreaching its shoreline,
doesn't devour the flatlands with more violent haste
than young Laertes, at the head of a riot,
overpowers your officers. The rabble call him lord;
and, as if the world were only now beginning,
the past forgotten, custom unknown
(the things that confirm and prop up every word),
they cry 'Let us choose! Laertes shall be king!'
Caps, hands, and tongues applaud it to the clouds:
'Laertes shall be king, Laertes king!'

QUEEN
How cheerfully they bay on the false trail!
Oh, you're running backward, you false Danish dogs!
[_A noise within._]

KING
The doors are broken in.
Enter Laertes, armed; Danes following.

LAERTES
Where is this king?—Sirs, all of you, stay outside.

DANES
No, let's come in.

LAERTES
I beg you, give me leave.

DANES
We will, we will.
[_They retire without the door._]

LAERTES
I thank you. Guard the door. O you vile king,
give me my father!

QUEEN
Calmly, good Laertes.

LAERTES
That drop of blood that's calm proclaims me bastard,
cries 'cuckold' to my father, brands 'harlot'
even here, between the chaste, unstained brow
of my true mother.

KING
What's the reason, Laertes,
that your rebellion looks so monstrous?—
Let him go, Gertrude. Do not fear for our person.
There is such divinity that hedges a king
that treason can only peep at what it wants,
and acts little of its will.—Tell me, Laertes,
why you're so enraged.—Let him go, Gertrude.—
Speak, man.

LAERTES
Where is my father?

KING
Dead.

QUEEN
But not by his hand.

KING
Let him ask his fill.

LAERTES
How did he come to die? I won't be played with.
To hell with allegiance! Vows, to the blackest devil!
Conscience and grace, down to the deepest pit!
I dare damnation. Here's where I take my stand:
that both worlds, this and the next, I count as nothing—
let come what comes; I'll only be revenged,
and most thoroughly, for my father.

KING
Who shall stop you?

LAERTES
My own will—not all the world.
And as for my means, I'll manage them so well
that they'll go far with little.

KING
Good Laertes,
if you want to know the truth
of your dear father's death—is it written in your revenge
that you'll sweep the board clean, drawing in friend and foe,
winner and loser alike?

LAERTES
None but his enemies.

KING
Will you know them, then?

LAERTES
To his good friends I'll open my arms this wide;
and, like the loving, life-giving pelican,
feed them with my own blood.

KING
Why, now you speak
like a good son and a true gentleman.
That I am guiltless of your father's death,
and grieve for it most deeply,
shall come as clear to your judgment
as daylight to your eye.

DANES
[_Within._] Let her come in.

LAERTES
What now! What noise is that?
Re-enter Ophelia, fantastically dressed with straws and flowers.

O heat, dry up my brains! Tears seven times salt,
burn out the sight and power of my eyes!
By heaven, your madness shall be repaid by weight,
till our scale tips the beam. O rose of May!
Dear maid, kind sister, sweet Ophelia!
O heavens, is it possible a young girl's wits
should be as mortal as an old man's life?
Nature is refined in love, and where it's refined,
it sends some precious part of itself
after the thing it loves.

OPHELIA
[_Sings._]
They bore him barefaced on the bier,
hey non nonny, nonny, hey nonny,
and on his grave rained many a tear—
Fare you well, my dove!

LAERTES
If you had your wits, and were urging me to revenge,
it could not move me more than this.

OPHELIA
You must sing 'Down a-down,' and you call him 'a-down-a.' Oh, how the spinning-wheel suits it! It's the false steward, the one who stole his master's daughter.

LAERTES
This nothing's more than sense.

OPHELIA
There's rosemary, that's for remembrance; please, love, remember. And there are pansies, that's for thoughts.

LAERTES
A lesson in madness—thoughts and remembrance, perfectly matched.

OPHELIA
There's fennel for you, and columbines. There's rue for you, and here's some for me; we may call it herb of grace on Sundays. Oh, you must wear your rue with a difference. There's a daisy. I would give you some violets, but they all withered when my father died. They say he made a good end.
[_Sings._]
For bonny sweet Robin is all my joy.

LAERTES
Thought and affliction, suffering, hell itself—
she turns it all to charm and prettiness.

OPHELIA
[_Sings._]
And will he not come again?
And will he not come again?
No, no, he is dead;
go to your death-bed;
he never will come again.

His beard was as white as snow,
all flaxen was his head.
He is gone, he is gone,
and we throw away our grief;
God have mercy on his soul.
And on all Christian souls, I pray God. God be with you.
[_Exit._]

LAERTES
Do you see this, oh God?

KING
Laertes, I must share in your grief,
or you deny me my right. Go now and step aside;
choose whichever of your wisest friends you will,
and let them hear and judge between you and me.
If, directly or by some indirect hand,
they find us touched by this, we will give our kingdom,
our crown, our life, and all that we call ours,
to you, in payment. But if not,
be content to lend your patience to us,
and we shall work alongside your soul
to give it the redress it deserves.

LAERTES
Let it be so.
His manner of death, his obscure burial—
no trophy, no sword, no coat of arms over his bones,
no noble rite, no formal ceremony—
cry out to be heard, as if from heaven to earth,
that I must call it into question.

KING
And so you shall.
And where the guilt lies, let the great axe fall.
Please, come with me.
[_Exeunt._]
SCENE VI. Another room in the Castle.
Enter Horatio and a Servant.

HORATIO
Who are these men that want to speak with me?

SERVANT
Sailors, sir. They say they have letters for you.

HORATIO
Let them come in.
[_Exit Servant._]

I don't know from what part of the world
I'd be sent word, if not from Lord Hamlet.
Enter Sailors.

FIRST SAILOR
God bless you, sir.

HORATIO
Let him bless you too.

FIRST SAILOR
He will, sir, if it please him. There's a letter for you, sir—it comes from the ambassador who was bound for England, if your name is Horatio, as I'm given to know it is.

HORATIO
[_Reads._] 'Horatio, when you've looked this over, give these fellows some way of reaching the King. They have letters for him. Before we were two days out at sea, a pirate ship, very heavily armed, gave us chase. Finding ourselves too slow to outsail them, we put on a forced courage, and in the grappling I boarded them. In that instant they got clear of our ship, so I alone became their prisoner. They have treated me like merciful thieves; but they knew what they were doing—I'm to do them a good turn in return. Let the King have the letters I've sent, and come to me with as much haste as you'd flee death. I have words to speak in your ear that will strike you dumb; and yet they're far too small for the size of the matter. These good fellows will bring you to where I am. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern hold their course for England: I have much to tell you about them. Farewell.
He whom you know to be yours,
HAMLET.'

Come, I'll find a way for you to deliver these letters of yours,
and do it all the faster, so you can lead me
to the man you brought them from.
[_Exeunt._]
SCENE VII. Another room in the Castle.
Enter King and Laertes.

KING
Now your own conscience must seal my acquittal,
and you must take me into your heart as a friend,
since you have heard, and with an understanding ear,
that the man who slew your noble father
was after my life as well.

LAERTES
It's plain enough. But tell me
why you didn't move against these crimes—
so wicked and so capital in their nature—
when by your own safety, your wisdom, and everything else,
you were so strongly driven to it.

KING
Oh, for two special reasons,
which may, perhaps, seem weak to you,
but are strong to me. The Queen, his mother,
lives almost on his looks alone; and as for myself—
whether it's my virtue or my curse, be it which it may—
she is so bound up with my life and soul
that, as a star can't move except within its sphere,
I can't move except through her. The other reason
why I might not go to a public reckoning
is the great love the common people bear him,
who, dipping all his faults in their affection,
would (like the spring that turns wood to stone)
convert his fetters to graces; so that my arrows,
too lightly made for so strong a wind,
would have flown back to my own bow again,
and not where I had aimed them.

LAERTES
And so I've lost a noble father,
and had a sister driven to desperate straits—
whose worth, if praise may look back at what she was,
stood as the challenger on the height of the whole age
for her perfections. But my revenge will come.

KING
Lose no sleep over that. You mustn't think
that we are made of stuff so flat and dull
that we can let danger pluck at our beard
and take it for sport. You'll soon hear more.
I loved your father, and we love ourself,
and that, I hope, will help you to imagine—
Enter a Messenger.
Well? What news?

MESSENGER
Letters, my lord, from Hamlet.
This to your Majesty; this to the Queen.

KING
From Hamlet! Who brought them?

MESSENGER
Sailors, my lord, so they say; I didn't see them.
They were handed to me by Claudio, who got them
from the man who brought them in.

KING
Laertes, you shall hear them.
Leave us.
[_Exit Messenger._]

[_Reads._] 'High and mighty, you shall know that I am set down naked in your kingdom. Tomorrow I shall beg leave to see your kingly eyes; when I do, after first asking your pardon for it, I will recount the reasons for my sudden and most strange return.
HAMLET.'

What can this mean? Have all the rest come back?
Or is it some trick, and no such thing?

LAERTES
Do you know the handwriting?

KING
It's Hamlet's own hand. 'Naked!'
And in a postscript here he says 'alone.'
Can you advise me?

LAERTES
I'm lost in it, my lord. But let him come;
it warms the very sickness in my heart
that I shall live to tell him to his face,
'This is how you die.'

KING
If it must be so, Laertes—
and how else should it be? How otherwise?—
will you be ruled by me?

LAERTES
Ay, my lord—
so long as you don't rule me toward peace.

KING
Toward your own peace. If he's now come back,
recoiling from his voyage, and means
to undertake it no more, I'll work him
into an exploit, now ripe in my mind,
under which he can't help but fall;
and for his death no breath of suspicion shall stir,
but even his mother shall clear it of foul play
and call it an accident.

LAERTES
My lord, I'll be ruled—
all the more if you can arrange it so
that I might be the instrument.

KING
It falls out right.
You've been much talked of since your travels,
and in Hamlet's hearing, for a skill
in which they say you shine. The whole sum of your gifts
did not draw such envy from him
as that one did—and that, to my mind,
the least worthy of any.

LAERTES
What skill is that, my lord?

KING
A mere ribbon in the cap of youth,
yet needful too; for youth is no less suited
by the light and careless dress it wears
than settled age is by its furs and dark robes,
which speak of health and gravity. Two months ago
there was a gentleman of Normandy here—
I've seen, and fought against, the French myself,
and they ride well on horseback; but this gallant
had witchcraft in it. He grew into his seat,
and brought his horse to such wondrous feats
as if he'd been made one body, sharing half his nature,
with the brave beast. He so far exceeded my imagining
that I, in dreaming up shapes and tricks,
fall short of what he actually did.

LAERTES
A Norman, was it?

KING
A Norman.

LAERTES
Upon my life, Lamord.

KING
The very same.

LAERTES
I know him well. He is indeed the jewel
and the gem of the whole nation.

KING
He spoke openly of you,
and gave you such a masterful report
for your art and skill in self-defense—
and for your rapier most especially—
that he cried out it would be a sight indeed
if anyone could match you. The fencers of his nation,
he swore, had neither footwork, guard, nor eye,
if you opposed them. Sir, this report of his
so envenomed Hamlet with envy
that he could do nothing but wish and beg
for your sudden return, to play a match with him.
Now, out of this—

LAERTES
What out of this, my lord?

KING
Laertes, was your father dear to you?
Or are you like the painting of a sorrow—
a face without a heart?

LAERTES
Why do you ask this?

KING
Not that I think you didn't love your father;
but I know that love is born in time,
and I've seen, in cases that prove it,
that time wears down the spark and fire of it.
There lives within the very flame of love
a kind of wick, or charred snuff, that will dim it;
and nothing stays forever at one even goodness,
for goodness, swelling to excess,
dies of its own too-much. What we would do,
we should do when we would; for this 'would' changes,
and has as many slackenings and delays
as there are tongues, and hands, and chance events;
and then this 'should' is like a spendthrift's sigh
that hurts by easing. But to the quick of the ulcer:
Hamlet's coming back. What would you undertake
to show yourself your father's son in deed,
more than in words?

LAERTES
To cut his throat in church.

KING
No place, indeed, should give murder sanctuary;
revenge should know no bounds. But, good Laertes,
if you'll do this, keep close inside your room.
When Hamlet's back, he'll learn you've come home;
we'll set on those who'll praise your excellence,
and lay a double polish on the fame
the Frenchman gave you, finally bring you together
and wager on your two heads. He, being careless,
most generous, and free from all scheming,
won't inspect the swords; so that with ease,
or with a little sleight of hand, you may pick out
a blade without a button, and in a treacherous thrust
repay him for your father.

LAERTES
I'll do it.
And for that purpose I'll anoint my sword.
I bought an ointment from a quack,
so deadly that, just dip a knife in it,
and wherever it draws blood, no poultice so rare,
gathered from all the healing herbs
that grow under the moon, can save from death
the thing it merely scratches. I'll touch my point
with this contagion, so that if I graze him at all,
it may be death.

KING
Let's think on this further—
weigh what conveniences of time and means
might best fit our purpose. If this should fail,
and our intent show through a botched performance,
it would be better not attempted at all.
So this plan should have a backup, a second,
that might hold if the first should fail in trial. Soft—let me think.
We'll lay a solemn wager on your skill—
I have it! When, in the bout, you're hot and dry
(and make your passes more violent to that end),
and he calls for a drink, I'll have prepared
a cup for the occasion; just a sip of it—
should he by chance escape your poisoned thrust—
and our purpose will hold there.
Enter Queen.
How now, sweet Queen?

QUEEN
One woe treads upon another's heel,
they follow so fast. Your sister's drowned, Laertes.

LAERTES
Drowned! Oh, where?

QUEEN
There is a willow that leans over a brook,
showing its silver-gray leaves in the glassy stream.
There she came with fantastic garlands she had woven
of crowflowers, nettles, daisies, and long purples—
which coarse-mouthed shepherds give a ruder name,
but our cold maidens call them dead men's fingers.
There, on the drooping branches, climbing to hang
her crown of weeds, an envious sliver broke,
and down her weedy trophies and herself
fell into the weeping brook. Her clothes spread wide,
and, mermaid-like, for a while they bore her up;
during which time she sang scraps of old tunes,
as one incapable of her own distress,
or like a creature born and bred
to that element. But it could not last long
before her garments, heavy with their drink,
pulled the poor wretch from her melodious song
to a muddy death.

LAERTES
Alas, then, she is drowned?

QUEEN
Drowned, drowned.

LAERTES
You've had too much water already, poor Ophelia,
and so I hold back my tears. And yet
it's our way; nature keeps her custom,
let shame say what it will. When these are gone,
the woman in me will be done. Goodbye, my lord;
I have a speech of fire that would gladly blaze,
but this foolish weeping puts it out.
[_Exit._]

KING
Let's follow, Gertrude.
How much trouble I had to calm his rage!
Now I fear this will set it going again;
so let's follow.
[_Exeunt._]

books.label: Act V
paragraphs: SCENE I. A churchyard.
Enter two Clowns with spades, etc.

FIRST CLOWN
Is she to be given Christian burial, when she willfully seeks her own salvation?

SECOND CLOWN
I tell you she is, so dig her grave at once. The coroner has sat on her case and ruled it Christian burial.

FIRST CLOWN
How can that be, unless she drowned herself in self-defense?

SECOND CLOWN
Why, that's how it's been ruled.

FIRST CLOWN
It must be _se offendendo_, it can't be otherwise. For here's the point: if I drown myself on purpose, that proves an act; and an act has three branches. It is to act, to do, and to perform. Argal, she drowned herself on purpose.

SECOND CLOWN
No, but listen here, goodman digger—

FIRST CLOWN
Let me finish. Here lies the water—good. Here stands the man—good. If the man goes to the water and drowns himself, then, like it or not, he goes—mark that. But if the water comes to him and drowns him, he does not drown himself. Argal, he that is not guilty of his own death does not shorten his own life.

SECOND CLOWN
But is this the law?

FIRST CLOWN
Ay, indeed it is—coroner's-inquest law.

SECOND CLOWN
You want the truth of it? If she hadn't been a gentlewoman, she'd have been buried outside Christian ground.

FIRST CLOWN
Why, now you've said it. And the more pity that great folk should have the backing in this world to drown or hang themselves more freely than the rest of us Christians. Come, my spade. There's no older line of gentlemen than gardeners, ditchers, and grave-makers—they carry on Adam's trade.

SECOND CLOWN
Was he a gentleman?

FIRST CLOWN
He was the first that ever bore arms.

SECOND CLOWN
Why, he had none.

FIRST CLOWN
What, are you a heathen? How do you read your Scripture? The Scripture says Adam dug. Could he dig without arms? I'll put another question to you. If you don't answer me to the point, confess yourself—

SECOND CLOWN
Go on.

FIRST CLOWN
What is he that builds stronger than either the mason, the shipwright, or the carpenter?

SECOND CLOWN
The gallows-maker; for that frame outlasts a thousand tenants.

FIRST CLOWN
I like your wit well, in good faith. The gallows does well. But how does it do well? It does well for those who do ill. Now, you do ill to say the gallows is built stronger than the church; argal, the gallows may do well for you. Have at it again, come.

SECOND CLOWN
Who builds stronger than a mason, a shipwright, or a carpenter?

FIRST CLOWN
Ay, tell me that, and knock off for the day.

SECOND CLOWN
Marry, now I can tell.

FIRST CLOWN
Out with it.

SECOND CLOWN
Mass, I can't tell.
Enter Hamlet and Horatio, at a distance.

FIRST CLOWN
Beat your brains over it no more, for your dull ass won't mend his pace for a beating; and when you're asked this question next, say "a grave-maker." The houses he makes last till doomsday. Go, get yourself to Yaughan, and fetch me a tankard of liquor.
[_Exit Second Clown._]
[_Digs and sings._]

In youth, when I did love, did love,
I thought it was so sweet;
to pass the time—ah—to suit my turn,
Oh, I thought there was nothing so meet.

HAMLET
Has this fellow no feeling for what he's about, that he sings at grave-making?

HORATIO
Habit has made it easy work to him.

HAMLET
That's just it—the hand that does little has the more delicate touch.

FIRST CLOWN
[_Sings._]
But age, with his stealing steps,
has clawed me in his clutch,
and shipped me off into the ground,
as if I had never been such.
[_Throws up a skull._]

HAMLET
That skull had a tongue in it, and could sing once. How the rascal dashes it to the ground, as if it were Cain's jawbone, that did the first murder! This might be the head of a politician, which this ass now lords it over—one that would outwit God himself, might it not?

HORATIO
It might, my lord.

HAMLET
Or of a courtier, who could say, "Good morning, sweet lord! How are you, good lord?" This might be my lord So-and-so, who praised my lord So-and-so's horse when he meant to beg it off him, might it not?

HORATIO
Ay, my lord.

HAMLET
Why, just so. And now it's my Lady Worm's—jawless, and knocked about the skull with a sexton's spade. Here's a fine overturning, if only we had the knack to see it. Did these bones cost no more in the breeding than to be played at skittles with? Mine ache to think of it.

FIRST CLOWN
[_Sings._]
A pickaxe and a spade, a spade,
and also a shrouding-sheet;
Oh, a pit of clay to be made
for such a guest is meet.
[_Throws up another skull._]

HAMLET
There's another. Why may that not be the skull of a lawyer? Where are his fine distinctions now, his quibbles, his cases, his titles, and his tricks? Why does he let this rude knave knock him about the head with a dirty shovel, and not charge him with assault and battery? Hmph. This fellow might have been, in his time, a great buyer of land, with his bonds, his recognizances, his fines, his double vouchers, his recoveries. Is this the end of his fines, and the recovery of his recoveries—to have his fine head full of fine dirt? Will his vouchers vouch him no more of his purchases, double ones and all, than the length and breadth of a pair of deeds? The very title-deeds to his lands will scarcely fit in this box; and must the inheritor himself have no more, ha?

HORATIO
Not a jot more, my lord.

HAMLET
Isn't parchment made of sheepskins?

HORATIO
Ay, my lord, and of calfskins too.

HAMLET
They are sheep and calves who look for their security in that. I'll speak to this fellow.—Whose grave is this, sir?

FIRST CLOWN
Mine, sir.
[_Sings._]
Oh, a pit of clay to be made
for such a guest is meet.

HAMLET
I think it is yours, indeed, for you lie in it.

FIRST CLOWN
You lie outside it, sir, and so it's not yours. For my part, I do not lie in it, yet it is mine.

HAMLET
You do lie in it, to be in it and say it's yours. It's for the dead, not the living; therefore you lie.

FIRST CLOWN
It's a lively lie, sir; it'll jump back from me to you.

HAMLET
What man do you dig it for?

FIRST CLOWN
For no man, sir.

HAMLET
What woman, then?

FIRST CLOWN
For no woman either.

HAMLET
Who is to be buried in it?

FIRST CLOWN
One that was a woman, sir; but, rest her soul, she's dead.

HAMLET
How precise the knave is! We must speak by the book, or wordplay will be the ruin of us. By the Lord, Horatio, these three years I have noticed it: the age has grown so refined that the toe of the peasant comes so close to the heel of the courtier, it chafes his blister.—How long have you been a grave-maker?

FIRST CLOWN
Of all the days in the year, I came to it the day our late King Hamlet overcame Fortinbras.

HAMLET
How long ago is that?

FIRST CLOWN
Can't you tell? Every fool can tell that. It was the very day young Hamlet was born—he that's mad, and sent to England.

HAMLET
Ay, marry, why was he sent to England?

FIRST CLOWN
Why, because he was mad. He'll recover his wits there; or if he doesn't, it's no great matter there.

HAMLET
Why?

FIRST CLOWN
It won't show in him there; there the men are as mad as he is.

HAMLET
How did he go mad?

FIRST CLOWN
Very strangely, they say.

HAMLET
How strangely?

FIRST CLOWN
Faith, by losing his wits.

HAMLET
On what grounds?

FIRST CLOWN
Why, here in Denmark. I have been sexton here, man and boy, thirty years.

HAMLET
